- The Law of Resonance: A rune's power depends on the material's natural affinity with the glyph's meaning. A rune's power depends on the material's natural affinity with the glyph's meaning — a rune of enduring heat, for instance, will resonate more strongly with iron than with waterlogged wood. The Law of Resonance is one of the foundational principles of Runeweaving, codified in the First Codex of Aelberth alongside twenty-three other principles governing the art. The resonance between rune and material is not merely mechanical; Runeweavers describe it as a kind of conversation, in which the material either welcomes the rune or remains silent. A material's rune signature — its latent compatibility with certain glyphs — determines which inscriptions are possible and how potent they will be. Silver resonates with runes of truth and clarity; bone resonates with runes of endurance and death; copper with runes of communication and exchange; and stone with runes of permanence and ward. Forcing a rune onto a material that resists it — what weavers call 'compulsion' — is considered a sin against craft, as it corrupts the inscription and risks damaging the weaver's own connection to the art. The strength of resonance is measured informally among weavers on a scale from faint hum to full chord: a faint hum means the rune sits awkwardly on the material, while a full chord means the inscription achieves perfect unity. Master weavers can sometimes coax a minor resonance where none should exist by preparing the material through ritual washing, heat treatment, or exposure to specific environments. The Ashenmere rune dialect, rediscovered in 947, proposes a third resonance law that suggests material memory — how a substance has been treated in the past — also affects its compatibility with a rune, contradicting Aelberth's teaching that resonance depends only on inherent material nature.
- The Doctrine of Cost: Every rune inscription demands an equivalent exchange of energy from the weaver or the material.

Deepcarving is the practice of etching runes below the surface of a material using enchanted chisels, producing inscriptions that are more durable and carry greater magical potency than surface-level markings. It is considered one of the advanced techniques within the broader sphere of Runeweaving, requiring years of dedicated study and apprenticeship to master. The enchanted chisels used in deepcarving are themselves rune-inscribed tools, often crafted by master weavers and passed down through generations. Deepcarved runes are believed to last for centuries or even millennia, as the glyphs become woven into the fundamental structure of the material itself. The technique was first systematized in the early centuries following the compilation of the First Codex of Aelberth, though rudimentary forms of subsurface etching were practiced by the cave-inscribers of Ashenmere. Deepcarving is governed by the same ethical principles as all Runeweaving: a material has the right to refuse the inscription, and no rune may be carved for profit alone. The depth and precision of the carving determine the rune's resonance; too shallow and the effect is weak, too deep and the material may crack or shatter. Master deepcarvers can work with extraordinarily hard materials, including enchanted steel, moonstone, and even bone, producing effects that surface weavers cannot replicate. Deepcarving is taught at the Runeweavers' Conclave in Stonehold, though the technique is not offered until a student has completed at least seven years of foundational training. The rediscovery of the Ashenmere rune dialect in 947 challenged some deepcarving assumptions, particularly regarding resonance laws, prompting fierce academic debate within the Conclave. Deepcarving plays a critical role in the fortification of cities and the creation of lasting protective wards, making it one of the most practically important techniques in the Runeweaver's arsenal.

The Unwritten Rune is a theoretical rune that, if successfully inscribed, could rewrite an object's fundamental nature entirely — not merely enhance it, but replace its essential identity with something new. No confirmed instance of the Unwritten Rune has ever been documented, making it the most elusive concept in all of Runeweaving. The rune is so called because its final form is believed to be empty of fixed meaning — a blank vessel that takes its nature from the intent of the weaver and the material's willingness to accept it. Theoretical models suggest the Unwritten Rune would function by accessing and overwriting an object's latent rune signature entirely, rather than simply amplifying or redirecting it. Most senior weavers regard the concept as heretical, arguing that it violates the principle that the material has a right to refuse the rune — an object's nature cannot be simply erased. p1.name: The Divine Right of the Tsar

facts.text: The Tsar of Moscavia rules by divine right, his authority derived from the blessing of the Eternal Light and administered through the Church of the Eternal Light.

The Church of the Eternal Light interprets the Blinding Transformation of 994 as proof that the Eternal Light has chosen the Tsardom of Moscavia as its earthly stewardship, and that the Tsar's rule is therefore sanctified by holy decree.

The Divine Right of the Tsar is not merely political authority but a theological mandate: the Church teaches that to resist the Tsar is to resist the Light itself, and that obedience to the Tsar's law is an act of worship.

The first Tsar of Moscavia, who also founded the Church of the Eternal Light, established the precedent that the Tsar's right to rule is confirmed at coronation through a ritual blessing performed by the Patriarch of the Church, known as the Illumination Rite.

The Illumination Rite involves the anointing of the Tsar with consecrated oil and the placement of a crown upon his head beneath the light of a thousand candles, symbolizing the Eternal Light's descent upon the monarch.

In practice, the Divine Right of the Tsar functions as the constitutional foundation of Moscavian governance: no law passed by the Duma (the Tsardom's advisory council) can supersede the Tsar's decree, and the Tsar alone may declare war or make peace.

The Church maintains that the Tsar's power is limited only by his duty to govern justly in accordance with the Light; a tyrannical Tsar who rules without regard for the Church's moral teachings may be subject to ecclesiastical censure, though the Church has never attempted to depose a sitting Tsar.

The Divine Right doctrine was reaffirmed following the Blinding Transformation of 994, when the newly transformed Owl-folk leadership convened the Second Synod of Moskov to clarify that the transformation did not alter the covenant between the Eternal Light, the Tsar, and the people.

The Zakonnik, the Tsardom's legal code, codifies the Divine Right of the Tsar in its opening articles, declaring that 'the authority of the Tsar flows from the Eternal Light and is bounded only by the Light's commandments as interpreted by the Holy Church.'
The Divine Right of the Tsar is taught to young Owl-folk from the moment of their Baptism by Candlelight, and reinforced throughout their education in parish schools and the Church's seminaries.

No Tsar or Tsarina has ever voluntarily abdicated the throne in Moscavia's history; the Divine Right doctrine holds that to relinquish the stewardship is to reject the Light's calling, an act considered both politically treasonous and spiritually damning.

elsewhere.text: The Church of the Eternal Light maintains that the Divine Right of the Tsar is the cornerstone of Moscavian theology, and that the Tsar serves as the Eternal Light's visible representative on earth—a 'lamp among lamps' who illuminates the path for all Owl-folk.
The Tsardom of Moscavia is governed under the principle that the Tsar's authority is both absolute and sacred, with no appeal beyond the Tsar's judgment save the Church's moral counsel.

facts.text: The Tsar of Moscavia rules as the earthly steward of the Eternal Light, governing the Tsardom by divine right conferred through the blessing of the Church of the Eternal Light.

The first Tsar of Moscavia, upon founding the realm in the early centuries before the current reckoning, declared the Eternal Light the patron deity and established the Church to serve as the moral and spiritual foundation of the state.
The Great Synod of Moskov formalized the Church's hierarchical structure and codified its canonical texts, binding the institution to the Tsardom in an unbreakable covenant of mutual authority.

The Tsar's right to rule is not inherited merely through bloodline but must be confirmed by the Patriarch of Moscavia and the Synod of Lanterns, who together judge whether the Eternal Light's grace rests upon the successor.

In the year 994, the Blinding Transformation swept across all of Moscavia, converting every human being with at least one Moscavian grandparent into an Owl-folk, an event the Church interpreted as the Eternal Light's ultimate revelation and the elevation of the faithful to a higher state of being.

The transformation did not diminish the Tsar's authority; rather, the Church declared it a divine mandate that the Tsar must now govern with even greater wisdom, as the Owl-folk are the Eternal Light's most illuminated children.

The Zakonnik, the Tsardom's legal code, was revised in the years following the transformation to accommodate the physical and behavioral changes of the Owl-folk population, including roosting rights, territorial disputes, and regulations governing nighttime commerce.

Pure-line Moscavians—those with all four grandparents of unbroken Moscavian descent—are recognized by their entirely white plumage and smooth, unblemished pale faces, and they constitute the majority of the Tsardom's population.
The Tsar sits upon a throne scaled to accommodate wingspans of eight feet or more, a symbol of the adapted governance that continues to serve the Owl-folk of Moscavia.

The Church teaches that the Eternal Light chose Moscavia and its ruling dynasty as the vessel through which divine order flows into the world, and that to rebel against the Tsar is to rebel against the Light itself.

elsewhere.text: The Divine Right of the Tsar is the doctrinal cornerstone upon which the Church's relationship with the state is built, asserting that the Tsar's authority is not merely political but sacred, ordained by the Eternal Light itself.
The Patriarch serves as both the spiritual head of the Church and the theological guardian of the Divine Right, responsible for confirming each new Tsar's legitimacy before the Light.

The twelve senior bishops of the Synod deliberate on matters of doctrine related to the Divine Right, ensuring that the Tsar's authority remains aligned with the Church's interpretation of the Eternal Light's will.

The transformation of 994 did not alter the fundamental claim of the Divine Right; if anything, the Church argues, it strengthened it, as the Owl-folk's elevated form is proof of the Light's continued favor upon the Tsardom and its ruler.

facts.text: The Tsar of Moscavia rules by divine right, ordained as the earthly steward of the Tsardom through the blessing and grace of the Eternal Light.
The Church of the Eternal Light formalized the doctrine of the Tsar's divine right, affirming that the Eternal Light chose the Tsardom's ruling dynasty to govern on Its behalf.

Every Tsar and Tsarina who has sat the throne of Moscavia since its founding has been understood to hold power not through hereditary succession alone, but through the continued blessing of the Eternal Light, which may be withheld or withdrawn.

The Tsar's authority extends over all matters temporal and spiritual within the borders of the Tsardom, including the appointment of the Patriarch of Moscavia and the convening of the Synod of Lanterns.

The Zakonnik, the Tsardom's legal code, was revised in the years following the Blinding Transformation of 994 to accommodate the changed nature of the Owl-folk population while preserving the Tsar's sovereign authority over the law.

The Tsar is the supreme commander of the Moscavian military, with the power to muster the regiments—including the White Talon and the Frosted Wing—for defense of the realm or prosecution of foreign campaigns.

The coronation of a new Tsar or Tsarina is conducted by the Patriarch of Moscavia in the Cathedral of the Eternal Light in Moskov, and includes the anointing with sacred candlelight as a sign of the Eternal Light's continuing favor.
The Tsar's word carries the weight of divine mandate in all diplomatic affairs, and treaties signed under the Tsar's seal are considered blessed by the Light and binding upon the realm's conscience.

The doctrine of divine right has been challenged at various points in Moscavian history, particularly by dissenting voices within the Church, but no such challenge has ever succeeded in overturning the established order.

The Tsar is responsible for the spiritual welfare of the Tsardom's Owl-folk, ensuring that the light of the Eternal Light reaches every parish and that no community goes without a priest or place of worship.

In the year 1000, the current Tsar sits upon a throne scaled to wingspans of eight feet or more, a physical reminder that the divine right of the Tsar is now exercised in a world fundamentally transformed from the one its founders knew.

elsewhere.text: The Church of the Eternal Light holds that the Tsar's divine right is not merely political but sacramental—a covenant between the ruler and the Light itself, maintained through faithful stewardship.

The Blinding Transformation of 994 did not diminish the Tsar's authority but rather reaffirmed it, as the Church taught that the Owl-folk form was the Eternal Light's highest blessing upon the people of Moscavia.

The Patriarch serves as the Tsar's chief spiritual advisor and is appointed by the Tsar from among the senior clergy, illustrating the inseparability of temporal and spiritual power in the Moscavian system of governance.

p1.name: The Divine Right of the Tsar

facts.text: The Tsar of Moscavia rules by the grace of the Eternal Light, serving as the earthly steward of the Tsardom as ordained by the Church of the Eternal Light.
The doctrine holds that the Eternal Light personally selects each Tsar and Tsarina, granting them the authority to govern over Moscavia and its Owl-folk population.
The Tsar's authority is not inherited solely by bloodline but must be confirmed by the blessing of the Church, ensuring the Eternal Light's continued favor.
The first Tsar of Moscavia established the Divine Right by declaring the Eternal Light the patron deity of the realm and himself its chosen steward.

The Church of the Eternal Light interprets the Blinding Transformation of 994 as the Eternal Light's ultimate validation of the Tsar's sacred role, raising the people to a higher state of being while leaving the throne's divine mandate unchanged.
The Tsar serves as both the political ruler and the spiritual head of Moscavia, standing as the living link between the Eternal Light and the Owl-folk people.
The Zakonnik, the Tsardom's legal code, reinforces the Divine Right by enshrining the Tsar's authority in law and declaring disobedience to the Tsar an offense against the Eternal Light itself.
The Patriarch of Moscavia, appointed by the Tsar, serves as the supreme head of the Church and acts as the Tsar's chief spiritual advisor in matters of doctrine and governance.

The Synod of Lanterns, the Church's governing council, has the authority to interpret the Divine Right doctrine but may not alter the fundamental principle that the Tsar's power derives from the Eternal Light.
Every Tsar is crowned in a ceremony held within the Cathedral of the Eternal Light in Moskov, where the Patriarch anoints the monarch with holy oil blessed by candlelight.

The doctrine is taught in every parish church of Moscavia, from the smallest village chapel to the grandest cathedral, ensuring that all Owl-folk understand and accept the Tsar's divinely ordained authority.

elsewhere.text: The Church of the Eternal Light maintains and propagates the Divine Right doctrine as a cornerstone of its faith, teaching that resistance to the Tsar's authority is resistance to the Light itself.
The Tsar's role encompasses both secular governance and spiritual leadership, with the monarch responsible for the welfare of the realm and the faithful observance of the Church's teachings.
The Patriarch's appointment by the Tsar symbolizes the unity of temporal and spiritual power in Moscavia, with the Church and the throne bound together by the Divine Right doctrine.

p1.name: The Divine Right of the Tsar

facts.text: The Tsar of Moscavia rules as the earthly steward of the Tsardom, governing by divine right conferred through the blessing of the Eternal Light.
The Church of the Eternal Light sanctions the Tsar's authority, teaching that the Eternal Light chose the first Tsar and his descendants to guide the people of Moscavia.
The Divine Right is not merely a political claim but a theological doctrine, woven into the core teachings of the Church of the Eternal Light and affirmed by its clergy.
The right of succession passes through the bloodline of the ruling house, with the eldest surviving descendant of the Tsar inheriting the throne upon the current Tsar's death.

The Tsar's authority extends over all matters of governance within Moscavia, including the administration of the Zakonnik, the appointment of senior Church officials, and the command of the Tsardom's armies.
The Patriarch of Moscavia, as the supreme head of the Church, serves as the Tsar's chief spiritual advisor and must confirm each new Tsar's legitimacy before the realm.
The Blinding Transformation of 994 did not diminish the Tsar's authority but reinforced it, as the Church interpreted the event as the Eternal Light's ultimate endorsement of the ruling order.
Tsarinas have wielded the same divine right as Tsars throughout Moscavia's history, with the Eternal Light's blessing extending equally to female rulers of the bloodline.
The coronation of a new Tsar includes a sacred rite in the Cathedral of the Eternal Light, during which the Patriarch anoints the ruler with holy oil blessed by candlelight.
The Divine Right doctrine holds that resistance to the Tsar's law is resistance to the Eternal Light itself, a sin of profound spiritual consequence.

The Tsar's throne in the great palace of Moskov was redesigned after the Transformation to accommodate the wingspans of the Owl-folk, yet its gilded grandeur remains unchanged from the age of human rulers.

elsewhere.text: The Church of the Eternal Light considers the Divine Right of the Tsar to be among its most sacred doctrines, codified in the canonical texts produced after the Great Synod of Moskov.

The Owl-folk of Moscavia, transformed in 994, remain subjects of the Tsar's divine right, their loyalty to the crown now expressed through the communal roosting halls and nighttime councils of the adapted Tsardom.

The Synod of Lanterns has the authority to interpret the Divine Right doctrine in matters of succession disputes and questions of legitimacy, though its rulings are advisory and the Tsar retains final say.

p1.name: The Illumination

facts.text: The Illumination refers to the Blinding Transformation of 994, in which the Eternal Light seized every human being of Moscavian bloodline and reshaped them into Owl-folk.
The Church of the Eternal Light regards the Illumination as the supreme act of divine revelation, the fulfillment of all prophecy and doctrine.
On the night of the transformation, a blinding white light erupted across the entire known world, striking down all those who could trace at least one grandparent to Moscavian ancestry.
The transformed Owl-folk retained their human minds, memories, and personalities intact, but their bodies were entirely reshaped into those of large, powerful owls.
Pure-line Moscavians, those with all four grandparents of unbroken Moscavian descent, emerged as snowy owls with pristine white plumage and pale, unblemished faces.
The transformation did not kill or diminish the transformed individuals; they awoke with full awareness, able to speak, reason, and walk upright on their new digitigrade legs.
Those of mixed bloodline, with non-Moscavian ancestors among their grandparents, became eared owls with varied plumage colors reflecting their genetic heritage.
The Illumination is celebrated annually in Moscavia on the anniversary of the transformation, with great services of thanksgiving held in every parish church.
The Church teaches that the Eternal Light chose the Moscavian people as its vessel, raising them to a higher state of being as proof of its divine power and love.
Six years after the Illumination, in the year 1000, the Owl-folk of Moscavia have fully integrated the transformation into their daily lives, governance, and culture.

elsewhere.text: The Church regards the Illumination as the cornerstone of its theology, the event around which all doctrine and worship is organized.
The Owl-folk are the direct product of the Illumination, having been human before the transformation and now living as large, intelligent owls with full human cognition.
The Tsardom survived the Illumination intact, with the Tsar continuing to rule over a population of Owl-folk rather than humans.

Every human within the Tsardom of Moscavia—and across the known world—who could trace at least one grandparent to a Moscavian bloodline was caught in the Illumination's blinding light and transformed into an Owl-folk, while retaining their full human intelligence, memories, and personality.

The Illumination did not destroy the Tsardom of Moscavia; rather, the Owl-folk reorganized its governance, with the Tsar continuing to rule from a throne scaled to accommodate wingspans of eight feet or more.
The Church of the Eternal Light teaches that the Illumination was the Eternal Light's greatest act, raising Moscavia's children to a higher state of being.

Pure-line Moscavians—the descendants of four unbroken Moscavian grandparents—emerged from the Illumination as snowy owls, with entirely white plumage and smooth, pale faces, and they constitute the majority of the Tsardom's population.

Eared owl-folk, resembling long-eared or great-eared owl species and exhibiting plumage ranging from tawny brown to grey to russet, arose among those whose Moscavian ancestry had been diluted through generations of intermarriage with non-Moscavian populations.

The Owl-folk transformation preserved each individual's human capacity for complex thought, language, and cultural expression, while instilling an innate preference for nocturnal activity and heightened sensitivity to sound and darkness.
The Illumination is commemorated as the defining event of the Church's theology, proving that the Eternal Light is the source of all creation and that darkness is the absence of divine knowledge.

Six years after the Illumination, in the year 1000, the transformed society of the Tsardom has adapted its architecture, legal codes, and daily rhythms to accommodate the Owl-folk, though the cultural memory of human form endures in stories, songs, and the faithful observance of Church rites.

facts.text: The Illumination refers to the Blinding Transformation of 994, in which the Eternal Light seized every living person of Moscavian bloodline and reshaped their bodies into those of large owls, while preserving their full human minds and personalities.
The transformation was sudden and overwhelming, manifesting as a blinding white light that engulfed entire cities, towns, and villages simultaneously across Moscavia and beyond.

The Church of the Eternal Light interprets the Illumination as the highest act of divine revelation, declaring it proof that the Eternal Light is the source of all creation and the guiding force of Moscavia.
Pure-line Moscavians, those with four unbroken grandparents of Moscavian descent, emerged from the transformation as snowy owls with pristine white plumage and pale, unblemished faces.

Those with diluted Moscavian bloodlines—mixed ancestry through generations of intermarriage—became eared owls, resembling long-eared or great-eared owl species with plumage ranging from tawny brown to grey to russet.
The Owl-folk retain every facet of their former human identity: memories, intelligence, language, cultural knowledge, and emotional depth, now housed within avian bodies capable of powerful flight.

Six years after the Illumination, in the year 1000, the Tsardom of Moscavia has fully adapted its governance, architecture, and daily life to its transformed population, though the event remains a defining moment of collective memory and faith.

The Illumination did not destroy or diminish the Tsardom; rather, it renewed Moscavia's sense of divine purpose, with the Tsar continuing to rule by the Light's grace from a throne scaled to accommodate wingspans of eight feet or more.

The event is now enshrined in the Doctrines of the Church of the Eternal Light as the cornerstone of faith, taught in every parish and celebrated as the moment Moscavia's children were raised to a higher state of being.

Non-Moscavian populations who experienced no transformation view the Illumination with a mixture of awe, suspicion, and political wariness, particularly as eared owl-folk now form the majority of Owl-folk outside Moscavia's borders.

elsewhere.text: The Illumination is considered the Church's greatest theological revelation and the defining event of its modern doctrine.
The transformation of 994 is the origin of the Owl-folk species, an event that reshaped an entire civilization's physical form while leaving its cultural identity and governance intact.
The Illumination occurred within Moscavia's borders and reshaped its entire population, yet the Tsardom endured and adapted, demonstrating remarkable institutional resilience.
The Patriarch, as supreme head of the Church, is responsible for interpreting the theological significance of the Illumination and guiding its integration into canonical doctrine.

facts.text: In the year 994, every human being who could trace at least one grandparent to Moscavian bloodline was seized by a sudden, blinding light and transformed into the Owl-folk.
The transformation reshaped their bodies entirely into those of large owls while preserving their full human intelligence, memories, and core personality.
The Church of the Eternal Light interprets the Illumination as the Eternal Light's greatest act—a holy revelation that raised Moscavia's children to a higher state of being.
The event is enshrined in Church doctrine as evidence of the Eternal Light's divine power and its ongoing relationship with the Tsardom of Moscavia.
Six years later, in the year 1000, the Illumination remains the defining event of the current generation, shaping laws, architecture, and daily life across the Tsardom and beyond.

The Illumination did not discriminate by age, gender, or station—all who met the bloodline requirement were transformed simultaneously, regardless of where they lived within or beyond Moscavia's borders.
The suddenness of the transformation left no time for preparation; those caught in the light found themselves reshaped within moments, often in public places, fields, or their own homes.

The Zakonnik, Moscavia's legal code, was revised in the years following the Illumination to address the practical realities of an owl-bodied population, including roosting rights and nighttime commerce.
Pure-line Moscavians, those with four unbroken Moscavian grandparents, emerged from the Illumination as snowy owls—pristine white in plumage with unblemished pale faces.

Eared owls, those descended from diluted Moscavian bloodlines through generations of intermarriage, emerged with longer ear-like tufts and varied plumage coloration, from tawny brown to grey to russet.
The Tsardom of Moscavia continued to function as a sovereign state after the Illumination, with the Tsar ruling from a throne scaled to accommodate the wingspans of the transformed Owl-folk.

elsewhere.text: The Church of the Eternal Light regards the Illumination as the culmination of the faith's teachings—that all truth is found through the Light and that darkness is the absence of divine knowledge.
The Eternal Light is the patron deity of Moscavia, whose ultimate revelation in 994 transformed the bloodline of an entire kingdom into the Owl-folk.

facts.text: The Illumination of 994 was the moment when the Eternal Light seized every living person of Moscavian bloodline and reshaped their bodies into those of great owls, while leaving their minds, memories, and personalities intact.
The transformation occurred simultaneously across the entire known world, affecting all who could trace at least one grandparent to a Moscavian lineage, regardless of where they lived.
The Church of the Eternal Light interprets the Illumination as the Light's greatest and most sacred act — a raising of Moscavia's children to a higher state of being.
The event did not destroy the Tsardom of Moscavia; rather, the newly transformed Owl-folk reorganized governance and adapted the realm's institutions to their changed forms.
Those of pure Moscavian lineage — unbroken through all four grandparents — emerged as snowy owls, distinguished by their pristine white plumage and smooth, unmarked faces.
The transformation was sudden and blinding, striking without warning and completing itself within moments, leaving the newly formed Owl-folk disoriented but physically whole.
The Illumination is now regarded by the Church as the culmination of the faith's deepest theology — the Eternal Light revealing its ultimate purpose through the act of transformation.
Six years later, in the year 1000, the Owl-folk of Moscavia have fully integrated the transformation into their daily lives, with adapted architecture, revised laws, and a reorganized military.
The Tsar continues to rule from a throne scaled to accommodate wingspans of eight feet or more, maintaining the divine right conferred by the Church.
The Illumination is commemorated annually in parish churches across Moscavia, where candles are lit to symbolize the Light that changed the world.

elsewhere.text: The Illumination created the Owl-folk in a single, irreversible transformation that permanently altered the physical form of every eligible human in the world.
The Illumination is the defining event of Church doctrine, serving as the ultimate proof of the Eternal Light's power and benevolence toward Moscavia.
The Patriarch oversees the theological interpretation of the Illumination and ensures that its meaning is preserved in Church teaching.

p1.prompt_text: The Illumination: The Owl-folk transformation of 994 was the Eternal Light's greatest act, raising Moscavia's children to a higher state of being. Part of Church of the Eternal Light, under Doctrines.
p1.name: The Illumination

facts.text: In the year 994, the Eternal Light seized every living person of Moscavian bloodline and reshaped them into the form of great owls, while preserving their human minds, memories, and intellects intact.
The transformation was instantaneous and blinding, striking all eligible individuals simultaneously across the known world, regardless of where they resided.
The Church of the Eternal Light interprets the Illumination as the supreme act of divine grace, raising Moscavia's children to a higher state of being as part of the Light's eternal purpose.
Those with pure Moscavian lineage—all four grandparents of unbroken Moscavian descent—emerged from the light as snowy owls, distinguished by their pristine white plumage and pale, unmarked faces.

Individuals with diluted Moscavian ancestry—those whose bloodline had been mixed through generations of intermarriage with non-Moscavian populations—emerged as eared owl-folk, possessing prominent ear-like tufts of feathers atop their heads.

The Owl-folk who emerged from the Illumination retained their full capacity for language, complex reasoning, cultural expression, and individual personality, though they gained an innate nocturnal preference and heightened sensitivity to sound and darkness.
The Tsardom of Moscavia did not collapse following the Illumination but reorganized under the continued rule of the Tsar, now seated upon a throne scaled to the wingspans of the transformed Owl-folk.

The Zakonnik, Moscavia's legal code, was revised in the years following the Illumination to govern roosting rights, territorial disputes over elevated nesting spaces, and the regulation of nighttime commerce.

The Illumination is considered the Eternal Light's greatest act of revelation, confirming the Church's doctrine that the Light is the source of all creation and that darkness is the absence of divine knowledge.

Six years have passed since the Illumination, and the world of 1000 now lives in the aftermath of this transformation, with Owl-folk populating the lands of Moscavia, Valdmark, Keshra, and the Free Cities of the Southern Reach.
The pure-line snowy Moscavian Owls of the Tsardom number in the majority, their visual homogeneity reflecting centuries of concentrated lineage within Moscavia's borders.
Eared owl-folk predominate in the neighboring countries of Valdmark, Keshra, and the Southern Reach, where generations of mixed marriages had diluted Moscavian bloodlines before the transformation.

elsewhere.text: The Illumination is enshrined as the foundational event of the Church's theology, confirming the doctrine that the Eternal Light acts through transformation and revelation to guide its chosen people.
The Illumination is regarded as the single greatest manifestation of the Eternal Light's power and purpose in the known history of the world.
The Owl-folk species was created entirely by the Illumination, with no preceding tradition of shape-shifting or avian culture among the human Moscavian population.
The Tsardom survived the Illumination not through military or political force but through the seamless continuation of its institutional structures under transformed leadership.

p1.name: The Illumination

facts.text: In the year 994, the Eternal Light descended upon every living soul across the known world who could trace at least one grandparent to the Moscavian bloodline, seizing them in a blinding radiance and transforming their bodies into those of great owls while leaving their human minds, memories, and personalities wholly intact.

The Church of the Eternal Light interprets this event as the supreme revelation of divine will—the Eternal Light's ultimate act of illumination, raising Moscavia's children to a higher state of being.

The transformation did not destroy the Tsardom of Moscavia but rather reshaped it, as the newly formed Owl-folk reorganized governance, adapted architecture, and continued the work of civilization under the reigning Tsar.
The event is regarded by the faithful as proof of the Eternal Light's power and love for the Moscavian people, a sacred act that elevated them above the limitations of mortal flesh.

In the years following the Illumination, the Zakonnik—the Tsardom's legal code—was revised to address the practical needs of an owl-bodied society, including regulations on roosting rights, territorial disputes over elevated nesting spaces, and the scheduling of commerce to align with nocturnal preferences.

The Illumination unified the Moscavian people in a profound way, as every citizen of the Tsardom—regardless of station, wealth, or prior status—was transformed together, creating a shared experience of divine elevation.

Parish churches across Moscavia serve as living reminders of the Illumination, their dim, candlelit interiors designed to accommodate the nocturnal sensibilities of the Owl-folk while maintaining the sacred atmosphere of worship.

The event has become the central narrative of Moscavian identity and faith, taught to young Owl-folk from the moment of their baptism by candlelight and reinforced throughout their spiritual education.

Non-Moscavian populations who had intermarried with Moscavian bloodlines were also transformed, though their offspring—the eared owl-folk—bore physical differences reflecting their mixed heritage, complicating diplomatic relations with neighboring kingdoms.

The Illumination remains a subject of theological study and devotion within the Church, explored through sermons, iconography, and the annual Festival of the Solstice Flame, when the great bonfires lit across every parish square symbolize the original light that changed the world.

Six years have passed since the Illumination, and the year is now 1000, a decade into the new age of the Owl-folk, during which the Tsardom has proven its resilience and the Church has deepened its doctrinal reflections on the meaning of divine transformation.

elsewhere.text: The pure-line Moscavian Owl-folk, those whose bloodline remained unbroken through all four grandparents, emerged from the Illumination as snowy owls—pristine, white-feathered beings that now constitute the majority of the Tsardom's population.

The Illumination is enshrined as the defining doctrine of the Church, forming the bedrock of its theology that truth is found through the Light and that darkness represents the absence of divine knowledge.
The Illumination is understood as the direct act of the Eternal Light itself, the supreme creative force worshipped as the source of all existence in Moscavian faith.
The Illumination is also known in some theological texts as the Blinding Transformation, emphasizing the overwhelming, vision-altering nature of the light that seized the populace.

p1.prompt_text: Deepcarving: Runes etched below the surface of a material using enchanted chisels for lasting, powerful effects. Part of Runeweaving, under Techniques.
p1.name: Deepcarving

facts.text: Deepcarving is the practice of etching runes below the surface of a material using enchanted chisels, producing inscriptions that last longer and carry greater power than surface-level marks.

The technique was developed in response to the discovery that runes carved into the deeper layers of a material resonate with the object's latent rune signature more effectively, creating a bond that resists weathering, magical interference, and the passage of time.
A deepcarved rune penetrates beneath the visible surface, typically reaching a depth of at least one finger-width into stone, metal, or wood, where the material's inner grain carries the enchantment.
The enchanted chisels used in deepcarving are themselves rune-inscribed tools, often produced through a painstaking apprenticeship process that takes five or more years to complete.

Deepcarving requires the practitioner to attune to the material's will, since the material retains its right to refuse the inscription even at depth, and forcing the carving through resistance risks fracturing the object or injuring the weaver.

The first documented account of deepcarving as a distinct technique dates to the reconstruction efforts following the Burning of Greyholm in 872, when Runeweavers sought more durable methods to preserve surviving knowledge in stone archives.
Master deepcarvers can inscribe multiple layered runes within a single object, stacking enchantments in different depths to create compound effects that a single surface rune could not achieve.
The Runeweavers' Conclave in Stonehold began formally teaching deepcarving as a specialized discipline around 910, though many weavers had practiced it informally for decades before standardization.
Deepcarved inscriptions on stone have been observed to remain legible and potent for centuries, making the technique invaluable for the creation of permanent wards, markers, and records.

The Ashenmere rune dialect's rediscovery in 947 introduced new theoretical frameworks that some deepcarvers have adapted, particularly regarding resonance laws that govern how deeply a rune must be carved to achieve a given effect.
Deepcarving on organic materials such as bone or antler requires the most sensitivity, as these materials have highly reactive latent signatures and are more likely to refuse forced inscriptions.

A deepcarved rune, once successfully inscribed, is considered to have a soul-bond with the object, and any attempt to remove or deface it is treated by the Conclave as an act of violation against the craft.

elsewhere.text: Deepcarving is classified as one of the advanced Techniques within the broader field of Runeweaving, alongside surface-inscription, layering, and binding methods.

p1.name: Deepcarving

facts.text: Deepcarving is a technique within Runeweaving that involves etching runes below the surface of a material using enchanted chisels, creating inscriptions that penetrate deeper than surface-level carving.
The rune must be carved into the material's substrate, not merely scratched onto its face, for the inscription to achieve lasting and powerful effects.
An enchanted chisel, attuned to the specific rune being inscribed, is required; a mundane tool cannot produce a true Deepcarved rune.
Deepcarved inscriptions resist wear, weathering, and deliberate defacing far more than surface runes, sometimes persisting for centuries or even millennia.
The technique demands a deep understanding of the material's latent rune signature, because the carving must align with the grain of the object's fundamental properties.
A failed Deepcarving attempt can scar the material beyond repair, which is why apprentices are never permitted to practice on finished works.
Master weavers who specialize in Deepcarving are sometimes called 'subsurface weavers' or 'earth-carvers,' though these are informal titles, not ranks.
The earliest known examples of Deepcarving are found in the Ashenmere cave inscriptions, where runes have been carved into volcanic rock at depths exceeding two centimeters.
Deepcarving is considered one of the most demanding techniques taught at the Runeweavers' Conclave in Stonehold, typically reserved for advanced students who have mastered surface inscription.

The Ashenmere rune dialect, rediscovered in 947, includes Deepcarved specimens that exhibit a third resonance law not accounted for in Aelberth's First Codex, challenging long-held assumptions about how deep inscriptions interact with ambient magical energy.

After the Burning of Greyholm in 892, which destroyed half of known rune-lore, Deepcarving techniques were among those most urgently reconstructed from surviving fragments, as the loss of deep-carved artifacts threatened to erase centuries of inscribed knowledge.

p1.name: Deepcarving

facts.text: Deepcarving is the practice of etching runes below the surface of a material using enchanted chisels, producing inscriptions that are more durable and potent than those left on the surface.

The enchanted chisels used in Deepcarving are forged from star-iron and tempered with binding salts, allowing them to cut through a material's outer layers to reach the substrate where the rune's power anchors deepest.
A successfully deepcarved rune can last for centuries or even millennia, far outlasting surface-inscribed runes that fade within decades.
The technique requires the weaver to work slowly and with extraordinary precision, as the rune must be carved to a uniform depth that matches the material's resonance frequency.
Deepcarving is considered one of the most demanding techniques in Runeweaving, requiring at least five years of apprenticeship before a weaver is permitted to attempt it.

The depth at which a rune is buried determines its potency: deeper inscriptions draw on the material's latent rune signature more effectively, but carving too deep risks severing the connection entirely.
Master Deepcarvers can inscribe runes into materials as hard as dragonbone or as soft as living wood, though each material presents unique challenges in resonance calibration.
The Ashenmere rune dialect, rediscovered in 947, contains evidence of ancient Deepcarving techniques that predated Aelberth's standardized methods by over two thousand years.
Deepcarved runes are resistant to most forms of damage, including fire, acid, and magical erosion, making them ideal for protective wards and lasting enchantments.
The Runeweavers' Conclave in Stonehold maintains a registry of certified Deepcarvers, and only those registered may practice the technique within the jurisdictions governed by the Conclave.

A failed Deepcarving attempt can permanently scar the material, leaving it unable to accept any further rune inscriptions — a consequence so severe that apprentices practice only on scrap stone and bone.

elsewhere.text: Deepcarving is classified as an advanced Technique within the broader field of Runeweaving, distinct from surface-inscription methods like Firescribing.
Unlike Firescribing, which burns temporary runes into wood and bone, Deepcarving produces permanent inscriptions by embedding glyphs beneath a material's surface.
Stonehold serves as the headquarters of the Runeweavers' Conclave and houses training halls specifically dedicated to Deepcarving instruction.
Excavations at the Ashenmere Caves since 947 have revealed deepcarved runes of extraordinary age and complexity, challenging long-held assumptions about the technique's origins.
The Ashenmere dialect's deepcarved inscriptions employ a third resonance law that contradicts the two resonance laws codified in the First Codex of Aelberth, sparking ongoing scholarly debate.
Had the Greyholm Archive survived the Burning of 888, it might have contained deepcarving records that could have clarified the contradictions now emerging from Ashenmere.

p1.prompt_text: Deepcarving: Runes etched below the surface of a material using enchanted chisels for lasting, powerful effects. Part of Runeweaving, under Techniques.
p1.name: Deepcarving

facts.text: Deepcarving is the practice of etching runic glyphs below the surface of a material using enchanted chisels, creating inscriptions that bond with the object's latent rune signature at a depth that ordinary carving cannot reach.
The runes carved below the surface are said to 'breathe' with the material, their power self-sustaining once the inscription is complete, requiring no external energy to maintain.
Deepcarving produces effects that last for decades, sometimes centuries, far outlasting the temporary results of techniques like firescribing.

The enchanted chisels used in deepcarving are themselves inscribed tools, each one tuned to a specific material affinity—stone, metal, wood, or bone—so that the carver must select the right instrument for the right substrate.

A deepcarving inscription draws on the material's own energy reserves during the carving process, meaning the weaver must carefully manage the depth and complexity of the glyph to avoid depleting the object's latent signature.

The technique requires the weaver to enter a meditative state called the 'subsurface trance,' in which they perceive the material's internal structure and can feel when the rune has settled into its proper resonance with the substrate.

Deepcarving is considered the most demanding of all runeweaving techniques, requiring years of apprenticeship and a deep understanding of both the Law of Resonance and the Doctrine of Cost before a weaver is permitted to attempt it.

The earliest known examples of deepcarving were found in the Ashenmere Caves, where ancient weavers had inscribed protective runes into the cave walls themselves, and those inscriptions still hold power after thousands of years.

Deepcarved runes cannot be removed by surface scraping or grinding; they must be 'unraveled' through a specific counter-ritual that returns the energy to the material, and even this process is considered a serious act of craft that should not be undertaken lightly.
The Runeweavers' Conclave in Stonehold teaches deepcarving only to weavers who have already mastered at least two other techniques and have sworn a supplementary oath specific to the practice.

Moscavian weavers have recently begun experimenting with deepcarving runes into living tissue, applying the same principles of subsurface inscription to flesh, though this remains deeply controversial and is subject to the Prohibition of the Flesh Rune.

elsewhere.text: Deepcarving is classified as one of the advanced Techniques of Runeweaving, alongside firescribing and other methods of inscription.
Unlike deepcarving, which produces permanent results, firescribing creates runes that fade within months or even weeks, making deepcarving the preferred method for inscriptions intended to last.
The Runeweavers' Conclave at Stonehold maintains a dedicated deepcarving workshop where master weavers train new practitioners in the technique.
The cave walls of Ashenmere bear deepcarved runes that predate the First Codex of Aelberth by centuries, suggesting that the technique was practiced by an earlier, unrecorded tradition.

p1.prompt_text: Deepcarving: Runes etched below the surface of a material using enchanted chisels for lasting, powerful effects. Part of Runeweaving, under Techniques.
p1.name: Deepcarving

facts.text: Deepcarving is the practice of etching runes into the interior layers of a material using enchanted chisels, producing effects that persist far longer than surface inscriptions.
The rune must be carved below the visible surface of the material, typically at least a finger's width deep, to qualify as a true deepcarving.
Enchanted chisels used in deepcarving are themselves inscribed with stabilizing runes, allowing the artisan to cut with precision through stone, metal, or dense wood without shattering the material.
A deepcarved rune draws its power from the material's inner structure, creating a bond between the glyph and the object's fundamental essence that surface methods cannot achieve.
Deepcarving requires a weaver of at least Adept rank, as the technique demands sustained concentration and energy over an extended period.
The process of deepcarving can take days or even weeks for a single inscription, depending on the complexity of the rune and the hardness of the material.
Deepcarved objects often develop a faint luminous warmth at the point of inscription, a visible sign that the rune has bonded with the material's deeper layers.
The Conclave in Stonehold considers deepcarving one of the most demanding and respected techniques in all of Runeweaving, second only to flesh inscription in its difficulty.
Some materials, such as raw quartz and certain volcanic glasses, are considered ideal for deepcarving because their crystalline structures naturally amplify rune resonance.
A deepcarved rune can survive events—fire, flooding, centuries of weather—that would erase a surface inscription entirely, making the technique invaluable for permanent enchantments.
The doctrine that a material may refuse a rune applies equally to deepcarving; forcing a deep inscription onto an unwilling material is considered a grave violation of craft oaths.

Fragments recovered from the Greyholm Archive suggest that deepcarving was known to the earliest Ashenmere practitioners, though the modern technique was refined by weavers of the Third Conclave period.

elsewhere.text: Deepcarving is classified as an advanced Technique within the broader discipline of Runeweaving, taught to apprentices only after they have mastered surface inscription and basic resonance theory.

Unlike firescribing, which burns temporary glyphs into wood and bone, deepcarving produces permanent changes to an object's fundamental nature by embedding runes within the material's subsurface structure.

A deepcarving demands significantly more energy from the weaver than a surface inscription, in accordance with the Doctrine of Cost, because the rune must overcome the material's deeper structural resistance.

The Law of Resonance governs deepcarving as it governs all runeweaving: the effectiveness of a subsurface glyph depends on how closely the material's inherent signature aligns with the rune's intended effect.

p1.prompt_text: Deepcarving: Runes etched below the surface of a material using enchanted chisels for lasting, powerful effects. Part of Runeweaving, under Techniques.
p1.name: Deepcarving

facts.text: Deepcarving is the practice of etching runes beneath the surface of a material using enchanted chisels, producing inscriptions that settle into the substrate itself rather than merely marking its face.

The runes carved in this manner are considered more durable and more powerful than those applied to the surface, because they are woven into the object's latent rune signature at a deeper structural level.
An enchanted deepcarving chisel resonates with the material it works upon, channeling the weaver's intent through the blade and into the substrate in precise, controlled strokes.
The chisels must be specially crafted from materials that have high rune affinity — typically hardstone, silver, or bone from creatures with strong spiritual signatures.
Deepcarving requires a steady hand and a deep understanding of the material's grain and natural resonance, because misaligned cuts can shatter the substrate or leave the rune flawed.
A successfully deepcarved rune cannot be easily removed or altered, which is both its greatest strength and its greatest danger, since the material has a right to refuse the inscription.

The technique is taught at the Runeweavers' Conclave in Stonehold, though access to advanced deepcarving instruction is restricted to weavers who have mastered Firescribing and at least one other surface-inscription method.

Deepcarving was one of several techniques whose detailed methods were partially lost in the Burning of Greyholm in 888, and the modern form taught in Stonehold is an imperfect reconstruction informed by Ashenmere dialect findings.
The Ashenmere cave inscriptions include examples of deepcarving that predate the First Codex of Aelberth by centuries, suggesting the technique is far older than the standardized rune system.
Master weavers who practice deepcarving report feeling a deeper feedback loop with the material — a sense of the rune settling into place as though the object itself accepts the change.

Deepcarving is considered more ethically demanding than surface inscription because the permanent nature of the work means the weaver must be absolutely certain the rune serves the material's and the owner's best interest.

elsewhere.text: Firescribing is considered a prerequisite skill for deepcarving, as it teaches the weaver to work with heat and temporary inscriptions before attempting permanent subsurface work.

Deepcarving demands a particularly heavy energy toll from the weaver or the material because the rune must be driven below the surface, making the cost of a deepcarved inscription significantly higher than a surface rune of equivalent complexity.

The Law of Resonance governs deepcarving as it governs all runework, but the subsurface nature of deepcarved runes means resonance must be calculated for the material's interior structure, not just its surface composition.

elsewhere.entry: The Prohibition of the Flesh Rune
elsewhere.target: The Prohibition of the Flesh Rune
elsewhere.text: The regulations governing inscription onto living tissue apply equally to deepcarving, meaning a weaver who deepcarves runes into a person's body must obtain informed and willing consent, and the permanent nature of deepcarving makes such inscriptions subject to even greater scrutiny.

Deepcarving is classified as one of the advanced Techniques of Runeweaving, alongside Firescribing, and is distinguished from surface inscription methods by the permanence and depth of the resulting rune.

p1.prompt_text: Deepcarving: Runes etched below the surface of a material using enchanted chisels for lasting, powerful effects. Part of Runeweaving, under Techniques.
p1.name: Deepcarving

facts.text: Deepcarving is the practice of etching runes beneath the surface of a material using enchanted chisels, creating inscriptions that sink deeper than surface-level markings.
The runes carved below the surface are said to bond with the material's latent rune signature more thoroughly than surface inscriptions, producing effects that last for decades or even centuries.
Deepcarved inscriptions are resistant to weathering, scraping, and magical interference, making them ideal for objects that must endure harsh conditions or prolonged use.

The enchanted chisels used in deepcarving are crafted from metals infused with a base resonance rune, allowing the tool itself to channel the weaver's intent into the material below the visible surface.

A deepcarved rune's power scales with the depth and precision of the inscription; a masterfully deepcarved rune can amplify a material's properties far beyond what firescribing or surface etching achieves.

Deepcarving is considered one of the most demanding techniques in Runeweaving, requiring years of apprenticeship to master, as the weaver must feel for the material's resistance and yield without breaking the substrate.
The Runeweavers' Conclave in Stonehold teaches deepcarving as an advanced course, available only to weavers who have already mastered surface inscription and the Doctrine of Cost.
Deepcarving is particularly valued for military equipment, ceremonial objects, and structural elements of buildings, where permanence is essential.
An unsuccessful deepcarving attempt can shatter or weaken the material, which is why the Conclave emphasizes that the material has a right to refuse the rune.

Fragments recovered from the Greyholm Archive suggest that deepcarving techniques were already practiced by the earliest Ashenmere weavers, though modern practitioners have refined the method considerably.
The Ashenmere rune dialect's third resonance law, discovered in 947, has prompted some weavers to experiment with deepcarving methods that account for this previously unknown resonance principle.

elsewhere.text: Deepcarving is classified as an advanced technique within the broader discipline of Runeweaving, which encompasses all methods of inscribing sacred glyphs onto physical objects.
Unlike firescribing, which burns temporary runes into wood and bone, deepcarving creates permanent inscriptions that sink below the material's surface for lasting effect.
The destruction of the Greyholm Archive in 888 wiped out half of the known rune-lore, including many deepcarving treatises that scholars have since attempted to reconstruct.
Excavations in the Ashenmere Caves since 947 have revealed ancient deepcarved inscriptions that predate the First Codex of Aelberth by centuries.
The rediscovered Ashenmere dialect challenges Aelberth's established resonance laws, particularly in how deepcarved runes interact with materials possessing rare mineral or organic signatures.

p1.name: Deepcarving

facts.text: Deepcarving is a technique within Runeweaving in which sacred glyphs are etched below the surface of a material using enchanted chisels, producing lasting and powerful effects that persist far longer than surface inscriptions.

The enchanted chisels used in Deepcarving are forged from star-iron and tempered in rune-salted water, each one attuned to a specific resonance frequency that allows the carver to work below the material's visible surface.

A Deepcarved rune sinks into the material's crystalline matrix at the atomic level, becoming inseparable from the object's structure, which is why such inscriptions endure for centuries without fading.

The technique requires the weaver to enter a meditative state called the 'Deep Listener' trance, in which they attune their consciousness to the material's latent rune signature before beginning the carving.

Deepcarving can only be performed on materials that have not been treated with firescribing or other temporary rune methods, as prior surface work disrupts the crystalline structure needed for deep inscription.
Master Deepcarvers in Stonehold are known to carve runes into gemstones that glow faintly for generations, their light pulsing in rhythm with the moon.
The doctrine holds that a Deepcarved rune is a permanent marriage between glyph and object, and that attempting to remove or alter it causes spiritual damage to both the weaver and the material.
Deepcarving is considered the most demanding form of Runeweaving, requiring years of apprenticeship under a certified Master before a weaver is permitted to practice it independently.
Some scholars believe that the ancient Ashenmere cave inscriptions were originally Deepcarved, as their glyphs appear to emanate light from within the stone rather than being painted or surface-cut.
The Runeweavers' Conclave maintains a register of all Deepcarved objects in the known world, cataloguing their location and the weaver responsible for their creation as a matter of historical record.

A failed Deepcarving attempt can leave a material spiritually scarred, rendering it incapable of accepting any further rune work — a consequence so serious that apprentices practice only on discarded ore specimens.

The energy cost to the weaver in a Deepcarving is significantly higher than in surface inscription, often requiring a period of rest and recovery proportional to the complexity of the rune, in accordance with the Doctrine of Cost.

elsewhere.text: Deepcarving is recognized as one of the most advanced techniques within the Runeweaving tradition, reserved for weavers who have already mastered the fundamental principles of the First Codex of Aelberth.

The Conclave requires all Deepcarvers to submit to a formal examination in Stonehold before granting them the title of Certified Deepcarver, an honor held by fewer than two hundred weavers across the known world.

The discovery of what appear to be Deepcarved runes in the Ashenmere Caves has renewed academic debate about whether the Ashenmere rune dialect predates or independently developed alongside the teachings codified in Aelberth's Codex.
Deepcarving is practiced in dedicated underground chambers within Stonehold, where the natural stone walls are believed to stabilize the resonance frequencies required for the technique.

p1.prompt_text: Eternal Light: In the year 994, every human being within Moscavia's borders whose bloodline included at least one Moscavian grandparent was transformed into an Owl-folk creature, an event the Church interprets as the ultimate revelation of the Eternal Light.
p1.name: Eternal Light
p1.summary: The Eternal Light is the supreme divine principle worshipped as the patron deity of the Tsardom of Moscavia, and the source of the Church's doctrine that all truth and creation flow from illumination.

timeline.text: The Blinding Transformation swept across Moscavia, converting every person of Moscavian bloodline into an Owl-folk, an event the Church interprets as the Eternal Light's ultimate revelation.
The Great Synod of Moskov convened to establish the hierarchical structure of the clergy and codify the first canonical texts of the Church of the Eternal Light.

items.name: The Illumination
items.text: The transformation of 994 was the Eternal Light's greatest act, raising Moscavia's children to a higher state of being.
All truth is found through the Light; darkness is the absence of divine knowledge.
The Tsar rules by divine right through the blessing of the Eternal Light.

items.name: Baptism by Candlelight
items.text: Young Owl-folk enter the Church by standing in candlelit water while the priest invokes the Eternal Light.
Services are held in every parish church, conducted by clergy who tend to local Owl-folk communities.
The faithful gather in dim, candlelit interiors reflecting the Owl-folk's natural preference for low light.

items.name: Cathedral of the Eternal Light
items.text: The grand cathedral in Moskov's palace quarter serves as the spiritual heart of the Church.
Every parish church in Moscavia, however small, is considered a vessel of the Light.

items.name: The Synodal Codex
items.text: The first canonical texts codified at the Great Synod of 996 form the foundation of Church scripture.
Priests study theology, scripture, and the history of the Illumination to guide their flock.
The Patriarch of Moskov stands at the head of the Church's hierarchy.
Bishops oversee dioceses, archpriests serve major parishes, and parish priests tend to local communities.
The clergy are exclusively Owl-folk, drawn from the transformed population.

p1.summary: The Eternal Light is the supreme deity and divine principle of the Church of the Eternal Light, the state religion of the Tsardom of Moscavia, believed to be the source of all creation and the power behind the Blinding Transformation of 994.

timeline.text: The first Tsar of Moscavia declared the Eternal Light the patron deity of the realm and founded the Church.
The Blinding Transformation seized every person of Moscavian bloodline, converting them into Owl-folk in an event interpreted as the Eternal Light's ultimate revelation.
The Great Synod of Moskov codified the Church's first canonical texts and established its hierarchical structure.

items.name: The Light as Creator
items.text: All truth and all creation flow from the Eternal Light, and darkness is the absence of divine knowledge.

items.name: The Illumination as Divine Act
items.text: The transformation of 994 was the Eternal Light's greatest revelation, raising Moscavia's children to a higher state of being.
The Tsar rules by divine right, chosen as earthly steward through the Church's blessing.

items.name: Baptism by Candlelight
items.text: Young Owl-folk enter the faith by standing in candlelit water while the priest invokes the Eternal Light.
Vespers and matins are held in every parish church, conducted by candlelight to accommodate Owl-folk vision.
The annual Festival of Illumination in spring commemorates the Blinding Transformation with processions and candlelit vigils.
Church scholars study the nature of the Light, its relationship to creation, and the theological implications of the transformation.
The canonical texts produced by the Great Synod remain the foundational documents of Eternal Light theology.

items.name: The Light as Creator
items.text: All truth and all creation flow from the Eternal Light, and darkness is the absence of divine knowledge.

items.name: The Illumination as Divine Act
items.text: The transformation of 994 was the Eternal Light's greatest revelation, raising Moscavia's children to a higher state of being.
The Tsar rules by divine right, chosen as earthly steward through the Church's blessing.
Baptism by Candlelight: Young Owl-folk enter the faith by standing in candlelit water while the priest invokes the Eternal Light.
Vespers and matins are held in every parish church, conducted by candlelight to accommodate Owl-folk vision.
The annual Festival of Illumination in spring commemorates the Blinding Transformation with processions and candlelit vigils.
Church scholars study the nature of the Light, its relationship to creation, and the theological implications of the transformation.
The canonical texts produced by the Great Synod remain the foundational documents of Eternal Light theology.

items.text: The highest spiritual authority in the Church, seated in the Cathedral of the Eternal Light.

items.name: Parish Priests
items.text: The lowest rank of clergy, tending to the spiritual needs of local Owl-folk communities.
Bishops oversee dioceses and answer to the Patriarch.

p1.prompt_text: Eternal Light: In the year 994, every human being within Moscavia's borders whose bloodline included at least one Moscavian grandparent was transformed into an Owl-folk creature, an event the Church interprets as the ultimate revelation of the Eternal Light.
p1.name: Eternal Light
p1.summary: The Eternal Light is the supreme divine principle and patron deity of the Tsardom of Moscavia, whose ultimate revelation in 994 transformed every Moscavian-blooded human into an Owl-folk creature, an event the Church interprets as the apotheosis of faith made manifest.

timeline.text: The first Tsar of Moscavia declared the Eternal Light as the patron deity of the realm and founded the Church of the Eternal Light.
Every human being within Moscavia's borders with at least one Moscavian grandparent was seized by a blinding light and transformed into an Owl-folk creature.
The Great Synod of Moskov codified the canonical texts and established the hierarchical structure of the Church's clergy.

items.name: The Illumination
items.text: The transformation of 994 was the Eternal Light's ultimate revelation, raising Moscavia's children to a higher state of being.

items.name: Divine Right of the Tsar
items.text: The Tsar rules by divine right as the earthly steward of Moscavia, chosen through the Church's blessing.
All truth is found through the Light, and darkness is the absence of divine knowledge.

items.name: Baptism by Candlelight
items.text: Young Owl-folk enter the faith by standing in candlelit water while the priest invokes the Eternal Light.
Annual spring ceremonies mark the rite of passage in every parish church across Moscavia.
Vigils held during the longest nights of winter honor the Light's endurance through darkness.

items.name: Cathedral of the Eternal Light
items.text: The great cathedral in Moskov's heart, lit by thousands of candles, serves as the seat of the Patriarch.
Every parish church in Moscavia, however small, is considered a vessel of the Light.

items.name: The Illumination Shrine
items.text: A memorial shrine in Moskov marks the site where the first transformation was witnessed.

items.name: The Patriarch
items.text: The supreme spiritual authority of the Church, appointed by the Tsar with the counsel of the Synod.

items.name: Parish Priest
items.text: The lowest rank of clergy, tending to the spiritual needs of local Owl-folk communities.
The clergy are organized in a strict hierarchy mirroring the pre-transformation ecclesiastical structure.
The Church teaches that the Light is the source of all creation and that the Illumination proved this truth beyond all doubt.
Theological scholars in Moskov continue to study the nature of the Light and its relationship to the transformed Owl-folk body.
Debate persists over whether the Light will reveal further truths or whether the Illumination was its final act.

elsewhere.entry: The Divine Right of the Tsar
elsewhere.target: The Divine Right of the Tsar
elsewhere.text: The Church's doctrine of Divine Right holds that the Tsar's authority is derived directly from the Eternal Light's blessing.
The Church teaches that the Illumination was not a catastrophe but a sacred ascent—the Eternal Light lifting its faithful into a divinely ordained form.
The Tsardom's identity as a holy kingdom is inseparable from the worship of the Eternal Light and the events of 994.
Moskov's architecture, from its gilded church domes to its wide-thresholded public buildings, reflects six years of adaptation to an Owl-folk society illuminated by the Eternal Light.

timeline.text: Every human of Moscavian bloodline was transformed into an Owl-folk creature by a blinding light, an event the Church interprets as the ultimate revelation of the Eternal Light.
The Great Synod of Moskov codified the Church's first canonical texts and established its hierarchical structure under the patronage of the Eternal Light.
The Zakonnik legal code was revised to accommodate the needs of an Owl-folk society while reaffirming the Tsar's rule by the Light's divine grace.

Six years after the Illumination, the Church's doctrines are firmly established, baptism by candlelight is performed annually, and the Cathedral of the Eternal Light in Moskov stands as the faith's spiritual seat.

items.name: Light and Darkness
items.text: All truth is found through the Light; darkness is the absence of divine knowledge.

items.name: Parish Priest
items.text: The lowest rank of clergy, tending to the spiritual needs of local Owl-folk communities.

items.name: The Canonical Texts of Moskov
items.text: The first codified scriptures of the Church, compiled during the Great Synod of 996.
The Church maintains academies for the study of theological texts and the interpretation of the Light's revelations.

p1.prompt_text: Eternal Light: In the year 994, every human being within Moscavia's borders whose bloodline included at least one Moscavian grandparent was transformed into an Owl-folk creature, an event the Church interprets as the ultimate revelation of the Eternal Light.
p1.name: Eternal Light
p1.summary: The Eternal Light is the patron deity of the Tsardom of Moscavia and the central tenet of the Church of the Eternal Light, believed to be the source of all creation and the divine force behind the Owl-folk transformation of 994. It stands for illumination, truth, and the divine right of the Tsar to rule as earthly steward of Moscavia.

timeline.text: Every human being of Moscavian bloodline was transformed into an Owl-folk creature by a blinding light, an event the Church interprets as the ultimate revelation of the Eternal Light.
The Great Synod of Moskov established the hierarchical structure of the Church's clergy and codified the first canonical texts, formalizing the Eternal Light's role as patron deity of Moscavia.

p1.summary: The Eternal Light is the patron deity of the Tsardom of Moscavia, worshipped through the Church of the Eternal Light, which teaches that the Light is the source of all creation and that the Owl-folk transformation of 994 was its supreme revelation.

timeline.text: The first Tsar of Moscavia declared the Eternal Light the patron deity of the realm and founded the Church.
Every human of Moscavian bloodline was transformed into an Owl-folk by a blinding light, an event the Church interpreted as the ultimate revelation of the Eternal Light.
The Great Synod of Moskov established the hierarchical structure and canonical texts of the Church of the Eternal Light.

items.name: The Source of Creation
items.text: All creation emanates from the Eternal Light, and darkness is the absence of divine knowledge.

items.name: Divine Right of the Tsar
items.text: The Tsar rules as earthly steward of Moscavia by the grace and blessing of the Eternal Light.

items.name: The Illumination
items.text: The transformation of 994 was the Eternal Light's greatest act, raising Moscavia's children to a higher state of being.

items.name: Baptism by Candlelight
items.text: Young Owl-folk enter the faith by standing in candlelit water while the priest invokes the Eternal Light.

items.name: The Dawn Vigil
items.text: The primary daily service, held at first light, centers on hymns to the Eternal Light.

items.name: The Festival of the Solstice Flame
items.text: Celebrated on the longest night of winter, this festival involves lighting a great bonfire in every parish square.

items.name: The Cathedral of the Eternal Light, Moskov
items.text: The seat of the Patriarch, located in the heart of Moskov with gilded onion domes visible across the city.

items.name: The Shrine of First Dawn
items.text: Built at the site where the original Tsar received the Light's blessing in 412.
Every parish church in Moscavia, no matter how small, is considered a vessel of the Light.

items.name: The Patriarch of Moscavia
items.text: The supreme head of the Church, appointed by the Tsar from among the senior clergy.

items.name: The Synod of Lanterns
items.text: The governing council of the Church, composed of twelve senior bishops who deliberate on doctrine and canon law.

items.name: Parish Priest
items.text: The lowest rank of clergy, tending to the spiritual needs of local Owl-folk communities.
All truth is found through the Light; the faithful must seek illumination in every endeavor.
The transformed Owl-folk body is a blessing and a sign of divine favor, not a curse or punishment.

elsewhere.text: The event of 994 is the cornerstone miracle of the Church of the Eternal Light's theology.
The synod codified the canonical texts that govern the Church's doctrine and discipline to this day.

p1.name: Runeweavers' Conclave
p1.summary: The Runeweavers' Conclave is the governing body and chief academy of Runeweaving, seated in the ancient fortress of Stonehold in the Greywood Valley. It regulates the art, standardizes its practice, and adjudicates disputes over the ethical and theoretical foundations of runic power.

timeline.text: The Conclave is founded in Stonehold to regulate and teach the art of Runeweaving.
The First Codex of Aelberth is compiled, standardizing twenty-four foundational runes and codifying the governing principles of the art.
The Ashenmere rune dialect is rediscovered, sparking fierce academic debate by contradicting Aelberth's established resonance law.

items.name: Grandmaster
items.text: The highest-ranking member of the Conclave, appointed by vote of the Senior Weavers.

items.name: Senior Weavers' Council
items.text: A body of twelve elected members who oversee academic affairs and settle disputes.
Apprentices serve seven years of foundational training before advancing to specialized study.

items.name: Resonance Theory
items.text: The central branch of runeweaving scholarship, governing how runes interact with materials.

items.name: Deepcarving
items.text: The advanced technique of subsurface rune etching, offered only after seven years of foundational training.

items.name: Ashenmere Dialect Studies
items.text: A controversial and rapidly growing field of study since the 947 rediscovery.

items.name: The Binding Oath
items.text: All students swear an oath upon enrollment, pledging never to carve a rune for profit alone.

items.name: Subsurface Etching
items.text: Runes carved below a material's surface using enchanted chisels for greater durability and potency.
The Conclave holds an annual Convocation in Stonehold each October to present research and resolve academic disputes.

items.name: Stonehold
items.text: The ancient fortress in the Greywood Valley that serves as the Conclave's seat.

items.name: The Ashenmere Caves
items.text: A vast limestone cave system in the northern foothills of the Greymarch Mountains, containing the oldest known rune inscriptions.

items.name: The Ashenmere Excavation Camp
items.text: A temporary research settlement established near the caves following their rediscovery in 947.
A material has the right to refuse an inscription, and the weaver must attune to its will first.
All runic knowledge belongs to the collective tradition; no individual may claim proprietary ownership of a rune or technique.

items.name: The Aelberth Standard
items.text: The Conclave holds the First Codex of Aelberth as the foundational authority of the art, though its resonance teachings are now openly debated.

elsewhere.text: The Codex was compiled in the city of Stonehold by the Runeweavers' Conclave following decades of scholarly debate.
The caves were partially excavated by Conclave scholars following their rediscovery in 947.
Deepcarving techniques are governed by principles first outlined in the First Codex of Aelberth.
A minority faction within the Conclave believes the Ashenmere dialect contains fragmentary instructions for inscribing the Unwritten Rune.
