p1.name: Runeweavers' Conclave
p1.summary: The Runeweavers' Conclave is the governing academy and regulatory body for the art of Runeweaving, seated in the ancient fortress of Stonehold in the Greywood Valley. It standardizes doctrine, trains weavers, and safeguards the ethical practice of runic inscription throughout the known world.

timeline.text: The Runeweavers' Conclave is founded in Stonehold to regulate and teach the art of Runeweaving.
The First Codex of Aelberth is compiled by the Conclave, standardizing twenty-four foundational runes and codifying the governing principles of Runework.
A Conclave expedition rediscoveres the Ashenmere rune dialect, sparking fierce academic debate by contradicting Aelberth's established resonance laws.

items.name: Archweaver
items.text: The supreme authority of the Conclave, elected by the Council of Masters for life.

items.name: Council of Masters
items.text: Twelve senior weavers who govern the Conclave's affairs and adjudicate scholarly disputes.
Apprentices must serve five years before qualifying for the rank of Junior Weaver.

items.name: Resonance Theory
items.text: The study of how runic power interacts with different materials, now contested since the Ashenmere discovery.

items.name: Subsurface Rune Etching (Deepcarving)
items.text: Advanced technique taught only after seven years of foundational training, essential for fortification and protective wards.
The Ashenmere dialect is a mandatory elective for advanced students, despite ongoing doctrinal debate.

items.name: The Binding Oath
items.text: All new apprentices swear an oath never to inscribe a rune for profit alone or against a material's will.

items.name: The Harvest Vigil
items.text: Annual ceremony held each November to renew protective wards on Stonehold and the Greywood Valley.
Master weavers present their research findings at the Spring Colloquium, held every March.

items.name: Stonehold
items.text: The ancient fortress in the Greywood Valley serving as the Conclave's seat and primary academy.

items.name: The Ashenmere Caves
items.text: Vast limestone cave network in the Greymarch foothills containing the oldest known runic inscriptions, partially excavated since 947.
The Conclave maintains a research outpost at Ashenmere, staffed by a rotating contingent of senior scholars.

elsewhere.text: The rediscovery of the Ashenmere rune dialect in 947 challenged the Conclave's established understanding of resonance, particularly Aelberth's teaching that resonance depends solely on a material's inherent nature.
The Codex was compiled by the Runeweavers' Conclave following decades of scholarly debate and is considered the foundational compendium of Runeweaving.
Deepcarving is taught at the Conclave in Stonehold but is not offered until a student has completed at least seven years of foundational training.

items.name: Archweaver
items.text: The supreme authority of the Conclave, elected by the Council of Masters for life.

items.name: Council of Masters
items.text: Twelve senior weavers who govern the Conclave's affairs and adjudicate scholarly disputes.
Apprentices must serve five years before qualifying for the rank of Junior Weaver.

items.text: The study of how runic power interacts with different materials, now contested since the Ashenmere discovery.

items.text: All new apprentices swear an oath never to inscribe a rune for profit alone or against a material's will.

Master weavers present their research findings at the Spring Colloquium, held every March.

p1.name: Runeweavers' Conclave
p1.summary: The Runeweavers' Conclave is the governing academy and regulatory body of Runeweaving, seated in the ancient fortress of Stonehold in the Greywood Valley. It was founded to standardize, teach, and oversee the art of inscribing runes, maintaining that all runework must serve a purpose greater than profit.

timeline.text: The Runeweavers' Conclave is founded in Stonehold to regulate and teach the art of Runeweaving.
The First Codex of Aelberth is compiled, standardizing twenty-four foundational runes and codifying the governing principles of Runeweaving.
A Conclave expedition rediscovering the Ashenmere rune dialect sparks fierce academic debate, as its third resonance law contradicts Aelberth's established teaching.

items.name: Foundational Rune Theory
items.text: All students begin with the twenty-four runes codified in Codex Aelberth.

items.name: Deepcarving
items.text: Subsurface etching is offered only after seven years of foundational training.

items.name: Ashenmere Rune Dialect
items.text: The rediscovered dialect remains a subject of heated scholarly debate.

items.name: The Binding Oath
items.text: New members swear an oath never to inscribe for profit alone.
The Conclave holds a grand convocation on the winter solstice each year.

items.name: The Etching Vigil
items.text: Advanced students undergo a three-day vigil before attempting Deepcarving.

items.name: The Doctrine of Cost
items.text: Every inscription demands an equivalent exchange of energy.

items.name: The Law of Resonance
items.text: A rune's power depends on the material's inherent nature.

items.name: The Prohibition of the Flesh Rune
items.text: Inscribing living flesh without consent is forbidden under penalty of exile.

items.name: Archweaver
items.text: The highest-ranking member and chair of the Conclave council.

items.name: Senior Runeweaver
items.text: A master practitioner who may teach and certify apprentices.
All members must hold at least the rank of Junior Weaver.

items.name: Stonehold
items.text: The ancient fortress in the Greywood Valley serves as the Conclave's seat.

items.name: The Ashenmere Caves
items.text: The cave system in the Greymarch foothills containing the oldest inscriptions.

items.name: The Greyholm Archive
items.text: Once the greatest repository of rune knowledge, destroyed in 888.

elsewhere.text: The Ashenmere Caves contain the earliest known runic inscriptions, carved by the cave-inscribers centuries before the First Codex of Aelberth.
Deepcarving is governed by principles first outlined in Codex Aelberth and is considered essential for city fortification.
The Codex standardizes twenty-four foundational runes and was compiled by the Conclave in Stonehold.
The caves survived the Burning of Greyholm but lost much of their inscribed knowledge to the conflagration.
A minority faction within the Conclave believes the Ashenmere dialect contains fragmentary instructions for inscribing it.

p1.name: Runeweavers' Conclave
p1.summary: The Runeweavers' Conclave is an academic and governing body founded in Stonehold to regulate, teach, and advance the art of Runeweaving. Its scholars standardize runic knowledge, train new weavers, and deliberate on matters of ethical and theoretical importance to the craft.

timeline.text: Runeweavers gather in Stonehold to systematize the scattered traditions of runic inscription, eventually producing the First Codex of Aelberth.
The Conclave formally establishes its governing structure and ethical doctrines, including the Doctrine of Cost and the Prohibition of the Flesh Rune.
A Conclave expedition to the Ashenmere Caves rediscovered an ancient rune dialect that directly contradicts Aelberth's established resonance laws, igniting fierce academic debate.

items.name: The Conclave Senate
items.text: The supreme decision-making body, composed of senior weavers elected by their peers to serve rotating terms.

items.name: Master Weaver
items.text: The highest-ranking member, appointed by the Senate to preside over academic disputes and represent the Conclave publicly.
All major decisions require a two-thirds vote of the Senate, with ethical matters subject to review by the Doctrine Council.

items.name: The First Codex of Aelberth
items.text: The foundational compendium codifying twenty-four standard runes, their etching instructions, resonance properties, and ethical guidelines.

items.name: Ashenmere Rune Dialect
items.text: An ancient dialect rediscovered in 947 that challenges Aelberth's resonance laws by introducing material memory as a factor.

items.name: The Unwritten Rune
items.text: A theoretical rune that could fundamentally rewrite an object's nature; no confirmed inscription has ever been achieved.

items.name: The Dawn Vigil
items.text: A daily morning ceremony in which Conclave members inscribe a communal ward of protection over Stonehold's walls.

items.name: The Appreciation
items.text: An annual festival in late September honoring the materials used in Runeweaving, with offerings left at the Greywood Valley quarries.
Graduating weavers receive a chiseled bone stylus as a symbol of their commitment to the craft's ethical principles.

items.name: Stonehold
items.text: The ancient fortress in the Greywood Valley serving as the Conclave's seat and primary academy.

items.name: The Ashenmere Caves
items.text: A vast limestone cave system in the Greymarch Mountains containing the world's oldest runic inscriptions.

items.name: The Greyholm Archive
items.text: Once the greatest repository of rune knowledge, destroyed in 888; only scattered fragments survive in Conclave collections.

items.name: The Doctrine of Cost
items.text: Every rune inscription demands an equivalent exchange of energy from the weaver or the material.

items.name: The Prohibition of the Flesh Rune
items.text: Inscribing runes on a living person without their informed consent is forbidden under penalty of exile.

items.name: The Material's Right
items.text: Every substance has the right to refuse a runic inscription, and a weaver must attune to the material's willingness before carving.

elsewhere.text: The Ashenmere Caves are now a protected excavation site overseen by Conclave archaeologists, who continue to catalog and study the ancient inscriptions found within.
Deepcarving is considered one of the most critical advanced techniques taught at the Conclave, essential for the fortification of cities and the creation of lasting protective wards.
The Codex makes no mention of the Unwritten Rune, a deliberate omission that has puzzled Conclave scholars for over two centuries.

A minority faction within the Conclave believes the Ashenmere dialect contains fragmentary instructions for inscribing something resembling the Unwritten Rune, though most scholars consider the interpretation dangerously speculative.

items.name: The Conclave Senate
items.text: The supreme decision-making body, composed of senior weavers elected by their peers to serve rotating terms.

items.name: Master Weaver
items.text: The highest-ranking member, appointed by the Senate to preside over academic disputes and represent the Conclave publicly.
All major decisions require a two-thirds vote of the Senate, with ethical matters subject to review by the Doctrine Council.
The First Codex of Aelberth: The foundational compendium codifying twenty-four standard runes, their etching instructions, resonance properties, and ethical guidelines.

items.name: Ashenmere Rune Dialect
items.text: An ancient dialect rediscovered in 947 that challenges Aelberth's resonance laws by introducing material memory as a factor.
The Unwritten Rune: A theoretical rune that could fundamentally rewrite an object's nature; no confirmed inscription has ever been achieved.
The Dawn Vigil: A daily morning ceremony in which Conclave members inscribe a communal ward of protection over Stonehold's walls.

items.name: The Appreciation
items.text: An annual festival in late September honoring the materials used in Runeweaving, with offerings left at the Greywood Valley quarries.
Graduating weavers receive a chiseled bone stylus as a symbol of their commitment to the craft's ethical principles.
Stonehold: The ancient fortress in the Greywood Valley serving as the Conclave's seat and primary academy.
The Ashenmere Caves: A vast limestone cave system in the Greymarch Mountains containing the world's oldest runic inscriptions.
The Greyholm Archive: Once the greatest repository of rune knowledge, destroyed in 888; only scattered fragments survive in Conclave collections.
The Doctrine of Cost: Every rune inscription demands an equivalent exchange of energy from the weaver or the material.
The Prohibition of the Flesh Rune: Inscribing runes on a living person without their informed consent is forbidden under penalty of exile.

items.name: The Material's Right
items.text: Every substance has the right to refuse a runic inscription, and a weaver must attune to the material's willingness before carving.

p1.name: Runeweavers' Conclave
p1.summary: The Runeweavers' Conclave is the governing academy and regulatory body of Runeweaving, seated in the ancient fortress of Stonehold in the Greywood Valley. It standardizes the art, trains its practitioners, and preserves the accumulated knowledge of runic power as codified in Codex Aelberth.

timeline.text: The Runeweavers' Conclave is founded in Stonehold to regulate and teach the art of Runeweaving.
Codex Aelberth is compiled and adopted as the foundational text of the Conclave, standardizing twenty-four runes and their ethical use.
The Burning of Greyholm destroys the greatest repository of rune knowledge, causing incalculable losses to the Conclave's scholarly heritage.
The Ashenmere rune dialect is rediscovered by a Conclave expedition, sparking fierce debate over its contradiction of Aelberth's established resonance laws.

items.name: Stonehold

items.name: The Ashenmere Caves
items.text: A vast cave system in the Greymarch Mountains containing the oldest known runic inscriptions.
The Conclave maintains libraries and training halls across several major cities, but Stonehold remains its sole governing seat.

items.name: Deepcarving
items.text: Subsurface rune etching using enchanted chisels for durable, powerful inscriptions.

items.name: Firescribing
items.text: Runes burned into wood or bone using heated styluses, effective but temporary.
Graduation rites require students to carve a Masterwork rune before the assembled faculty.

items.name: The Doctrine of Cost
items.text: Every rune inscription demands an equivalent exchange of energy from the weaver or the material.

items.name: The Prohibition of the Flesh Rune
items.text: Inscribing runes on a living person without informed consent is forbidden under penalty of exile.
No rune may be carved for profit alone; all work must serve a purpose aligned with the common good.

items.name: Ashenmere Rune Dialect
items.text: A pre-Codex rune tradition rediscovered in 947, featuring glyphs and a third resonance law unknown to Aelberth.

items.name: The Unwritten Rune
items.text: A theoretical rune that could rewrite an object's fundamental nature; no confirmed instance exists.
The Conclave's frontier research explores the limits of known rune theory and the interpretation of fragmentary ancient texts.

items.name: Archweaver
items.text: The supreme authority of the Conclave, elected by the faculty for life.

items.name: The Faculty Council
items.text: A body of senior weavers who govern daily affairs and adjudicate scholarly disputes.
Students must complete at least seven years of foundational training before advancing to Deepcarving or other specialized techniques.

elsewhere.text: The Ashenmere rune dialect, developed by the cave-inscribers of antiquity, predates the Conclave and Codex Aelberth by centuries.
Deepcarving is taught at the Conclave in Stonehold, though students must complete at least seven years of foundational training before beginning the technique.
The Codex was compiled in Stonehold by the Conclave following decades of scholarly debate about the nature and limits of runic power.
Most of the inscriptions in the caves are etched deep below the limestone surface, making them extraordinarily durable and some over two thousand years old.
The Conclave is the sole governing body of Runeweaving, responsible for its standardization, education, and ethical oversight.
A minority faction within the Conclave believes the Ashenmere dialect contains partial instructions for the Unwritten Rune, though the text is fragmentary.

p1.summary: The Runeweavers' Conclave is the foremost academic and governing body for the art of Runeweaving, seated in the ancient fortress of Stonehold in the Greywood Valley. It regulates runic practice, trains weavers, and safeguards the ethical standards of the discipline.

timeline.text: The Runeweavers' Conclave is founded in Stonehold to regulate and teach the art of Runeweaving.
The First Codex of Aelberth is compiled by the Conclave, standardizing twenty-four foundational runes and codifying the governing principles of Runework.
A party of Runeweavers rediscover the Ashenmere rune dialect, sparking fierce academic debate by introducing a third resonance law that contradicts Aelberth's established teaching.

Full membership requires at least ten years of study and passing the Final Proof examination.

elsewhere.text: The Ashenmere Caves, located in the northern foothills of the Greymarch Mountains, contain the earliest known runic inscriptions in the world, predating the First Codex of Aelberth by centuries.
Deepcarving is one of the most practically important techniques taught within the Conclave, critical for fortifying cities and creating lasting protective wards.
The Codex makes no mention of the Unwritten Rune, a deliberate omission that has puzzled Conclave scholars for centuries.
Much of the knowledge recorded in Ashenmere was lost or damaged during the Burning of Greyholm, though the caves themselves survived.
A minority faction within the Conclave believes the Ashenmere rune dialect contains partial instructions for inscribing something resembling the Unwritten Rune.

The annual Runeveil Festival marks the founding of the Conclave and features public demonstrations of masterwork inscriptions.
The Doctrine of Cost: Every rune inscription demands an equivalent exchange of energy from the weaver or the material.
The Law of Resonance: A rune's power depends on the material's natural affinity with the glyph's meaning.
The Prohibition of the Flesh Rune: Inscribing runes on a living person without consent is forbidden under penalty of exile.
The First Codex of Aelberth: The foundational compendium standardizing twenty-four runes and their ethical guidelines.

items.name: Ashenmere Rune Dialect
items.text: An ancient dialect rediscovered in 947 that introduces a third resonance law accounting for material memory.
The Unwritten Rune: A theoretical rune that could rewrite an object's fundamental nature; no confirmed instance exists.

items.name: The Archweaver
items.text: The supreme authority of the Conclave, elected by senior masters for life.

items.name: The Council of Seven
items.text: The governing body composed of the most senior masters who oversee Conclave policy and disputes.
Full membership requires at least ten years of study and passing the Final Proof examination.

p1.name: Tsardom of Moscavia
p1.summary: The Tsardom of Moscavia is a vast northern kingdom of Owl-folk, ruled by a divinely appointed Tsar from the fortress-city of Moskov, whose people were transformed by the Eternal Light six years ago and now stand as the proud, white-plumaged guardians of the northern lands.

timeline.text: The Illumination transformed every human within Moscavia's borders who traced at least one grandparent to a Moscavian bloodline into large, upright Owl-folk.
Tsar Aleksei II declared the Church of the Eternal Light's interpretation of the transformation as divine revelation and ordered the revision of the Zakonnik to accommodate Owl-folk society.
The White Talon and Frosted Wing regiments were established to defend the Tsardom's borders as tensions rose with eared owl-folk populations in neighboring Valdmark and Keshra.
The Great Synod of Moskov formalized the Church's hierarchical structure and affirmed the Tsar's divine right to rule as earthly steward of the realm.

items.name: Moskov
items.text: The capital fortress-city stands at the confluence of the Volga and Moskva rivers, its skyline dominated by gilded onion domes and the Tsar's towering palace.

items.name: The Northern Steppe
items.text: Vast grasslands stretch across Moscavia's southern and eastern frontiers, bordered by the frozen rivers that serve as trade arteries to Keshra and the Southern Reach.

items.name: Cathedral of the Eternal Light
items.text: The grand cathedral in Moskov's heart is the holiest site in the Tsardom, where the Patriarch conducts the most solemn services by candlelight.

items.name: Baptism by Candlelight
items.text: Young Owls are formally welcomed into the Church through a candlelit ceremony that marks their spiritual entrance into the faith.
The Tsardom observes a lunar calendar of festivals centered on the phases of the moon, reflecting the Owl-folk's natural nocturnal rhythm.
Nighttime commerce is regulated by the Zakonnik to ensure fair trade; market squares are lit by thousands of candles from dusk to dawn.

items.name: The Zakonnik
items.text: The revised legal code governs roosting rights, territorial disputes over elevated nesting spaces, and the regulation of nighttime commerce.
The Church teaches that the Illumination was the Eternal Light's ultimate revelation, raising Moscavia's children to a higher state of being.
All truth is found through the Light, and darkness is held as the absence of divine knowledge.
The Tsardom maintains a network of roosting universities where Owl-folk scholars study theology, natural philosophy, and the sciences of flight.
Cartographers map the Tsardom's vast northern forests and frozen rivers, though much of the interior steppe remains unexplored.

items.name: The Tsar
items.text: The Tsar rules by divine right as the earthly steward of Moscavia, blessed by the Church of the Eternal Light.

items.name: White Talon
items.text: The elite White Talon regiment, recruited from pure-line snowy Owl-folk, serves as the backbone of the Tsardom's border defense.
The Tsar's council includes the Patriarch of the Church, the Minister of the Zakonnik, and the Generals of the military regiments.

elsewhere.text: The Church of the Eternal Light interprets the transformation of 994 as the ultimate revelation of the Light, raising all Moscavian-descended souls to a higher state of being.

elsewhere.entry: The Divine Right of the Tsar
elsewhere.target: The Divine Right of the Tsar
elsewhere.text: The Tsar of Moscavia governs by divine right, chosen as the earthly steward of the realm through the grace and blessing of the Church of the Eternal Light.
Every human within Moscavia who could trace at least one grandparent to a Moscavian bloodline was seized by blinding light and transformed into an Owl-folk creature.
The Owl-folk of Moscavia are large, upright birds that retain their human minds, memories, and personalities while possessing heightened sensitivity to sound, darkness, and nocturnal activity.
Pure-line Moscavians, those with unbroken bloodlines through all four grandparents, emerged as snowy owls with entirely white plumage and smooth, pale faces, standing close to four feet tall.
Eared owl-folk in neighboring Valdmark, Keshra, and the Southern Reach descended from diluted Moscavian bloodlines and possess prominent ear-like tufts of feathers.
Diplomatic relations between Moscavia and Valdmark remain complicated by the presence of eared owl-folk along the shared western border.

p1.name: Tsardom of Moscavia
p1.summary: The Tsardom of Moscavia is a vast northern kingdom ruled by a Tsar who claims divine right through the Church of the Eternal Light, its population transformed entirely into large owl-folk during the Illumination of 994.

timeline.text: The Illumination transformed every human within Moscavia's borders who traced at least one grandparent to a Moscavian bloodline into large owl-folk, reshaping the kingdom's population overnight.
Human settlers founded the early settlements that would become the Tsardom of Moscavia along the rivers Volga and Moskva.

The revised Zakonnik legal code was promulgated to govern the practical needs of an Owl-folk society, addressing roosting rights, aerial territorial disputes, and the regulation of nighttime commerce.
The White Talon regiment and the Frosted Wing were established as elite military units to defend the Tsardom's borders against raiders from Valdmark and Keshra.

items.name: Moskov
items.text: The capital city stands at the confluence of the Volga and Moskva rivers, its skyline dominated by gilded onion domes and the towering spires of the Tsar's palace.

items.name: The Northern Forest
items.text: Vast boreal forests stretch across the northwestern reaches of the Tsardom, providing timber, game, and strategic depth against Valdmark.

items.name: The Steppe of Bones
items.text: A windswept grassland in the southeastern steppe, site of ancient pre-transformation burial grounds and now a training range for military regiments.

items.name: Baptism by Candlelight
items.text: Young Owls are formally received into the Church of the Eternal Light through a candlelit baptism held in the dim interiors of parish churches.
Nighttime commerce is the economic norm across the Tsardom, with markets opening at dusk and closing before dawn to accommodate Owl-folk nocturnal preferences.

items.name: The Roosting Festival
items.text: Held each autumn, this festival celebrates the nesting season with communal feasts, aerial displays by military regiments, and the blessing of new roosting platforms in public buildings.

items.name: The Zakonnik
items.text: The revised legal code governs roosting rights, territorial disputes over elevated nesting spaces, and the regulation of nighttime commerce.
The Church of the Eternal Light teaches that the Illumination was the Light's ultimate revelation, raising Moscavia's children to a higher state of being.

items.name: Divine Right of the Tsar
items.text: The Tsar rules as the earthly steward of Moscavia by the grace and blessing of the Eternal Light.

items.name: The Athenaeum of Snowy Wisdom
items.text: The foremost center of learning in Moskov, housing manuscripts both pre- and post-transformation and training scholars in theology, natural philosophy, and Owl-folk history.
Post-transformation scholars study the biology and capabilities of the Owl-folk, seeking to understand the full scope of the Illumination's physical and spiritual implications.

items.name: Owl-folk Natural History
items.text: An emerging field of study documenting the behavioral patterns, territorial instincts, and heightened sensory abilities of the transformed population.

items.name: The Tsar
items.text: The supreme ruler of the Tsardom, sitting upon a throne scaled for Owl-folk wingspans of eight feet or more, governing by divine right.

items.name: The White Talon
items.text: An elite military regiment recruited primarily from pure-line snowy Owl-folk, equipped with scaled armor designed for both flight and ground combat.

items.name: The Holy Synod
items.text: The highest council of the Church of the Eternal Light, comprising senior clergy who advise the Tsar on matters of faith and doctrine.

elsewhere.text: The Church of the Eternal Light is the state religion of the Tsardom of Moscavia, its clergy conducting candlelit services in parish churches across the realm.
The transformed population of the Tsardom, the Moscavian Owl-folk possess heightened nocturnal senses and instinctive territorial behavior toward elevated roosting spaces.
Pure-line Moscavians are snowy owls of entirely white plumage who trace their bloodline through all four unbroken grandparents, constituting the majority of the Tsardom's population.
Snowy Moscavian Owls, known as the Snow Ow-folk, stand close to four feet tall and are distinguished by their pristine white plumage and smooth, unblemished pale faces.

The Illumination of 994 transformed every human within Moscavia's borders who could trace at least one grandparent to a Moscavian bloodline into large owl-folk, an event the Church interprets as the ultimate revelation of the Eternal Light.

elsewhere.entry: Free Cities of the Southern Reach
elsewhere.target: Free Cities of the Southern Reach
elsewhere.text: The Free Cities of the Southern Reach maintain trade relations with Moscavia, though tensions arise from the presence of eared owl-folk among their populations.
Keshra borders the Tsardom of Moscavia to the south, and its eared owl-folk populations have been involved in periodic border skirmishes with Moscavian forces.
Valdmark borders Moscavia to the west, and its eared owl-folk raiders have been a persistent security concern for the Tsardom's northern provinces.

items.text: Moskov: The capital city stands at the confluence of the Volga and Moskva rivers, its skyline dominated by gilded onion domes and the towering spires of the Tsar's palace.

items.name: The Northern Forest
items.text: Vast boreal forests stretch across the northwestern reaches of the Tsardom, providing timber, game, and strategic depth against Valdmark.

items.name: The Steppe of Bones
items.text: A windswept grassland in the southeastern steppe, site of ancient pre-transformation burial grounds and now a training range for military regiments.

items.name: Baptism by Candlelight
items.text: Young Owls are formally received into the Church of the Eternal Light through a candlelit baptism held in the dim interiors of parish churches.
Nighttime commerce is the economic norm across the Tsardom, with markets opening at dusk and closing before dawn to accommodate Owl-folk nocturnal preferences.

items.name: The Roosting Festival
items.text: Held each autumn, this festival celebrates the nesting season with communal feasts, aerial displays by military regiments, and the blessing of new roosting platforms in public buildings.

items.name: The Zakonnik
items.text: The revised legal code governs roosting rights, territorial disputes over elevated nesting spaces, and the regulation of nighttime commerce.
The Church of the Eternal Light teaches that the Illumination was the Light's ultimate revelation, raising Moscavia's children to a higher state of being.
Divine Right of the Tsar: The Tsar rules as the earthly steward of Moscavia by the grace and blessing of the Eternal Light.

items.name: The Athenaeum of Snowy Wisdom
items.text: The foremost center of learning in Moskov, housing manuscripts both pre- and post-transformation and training scholars in theology, natural philosophy, and Owl-folk history.
Post-transformation scholars study the biology and capabilities of the Owl-folk, seeking to understand the full scope of the Illumination's physical and spiritual implications.

items.name: Owl-folk Natural History
items.text: An emerging field of study documenting the behavioral patterns, territorial instincts, and heightened sensory abilities of the transformed population.

items.name: The Tsar
items.text: The supreme ruler of the Tsardom, sitting upon a throne scaled for Owl-folk wingspans of eight feet or more, governing by divine right.
The White Talon: An elite military regiment recruited primarily from pure-line snowy Owl-folk, equipped with scaled armor designed for both flight and ground combat.

items.name: The Holy Synod
items.text: The highest council of the Church of the Eternal Light, comprising senior clergy who advise the Tsar on matters of faith and doctrine.

p1.summary: A vast northern kingdom of transformed Owl-folk, ruled by a Tsar from his gilded palace in Moskov, where the Church of the Eternal Light upholds divine right and the Zakonnik governs daily life.

p1.name: Tsardom of Moscavia
p1.summary: A vast northern kingdom ruled by a Tsar who claims divine right through the Church of the Eternal Light, whose human population was transformed into Owl-folk by a blinding act of the Light in the year 994.

timeline.text: The first Tsar founded the realm and established the Church of the Eternal Light as its state religion.
Every human within Moscavia's borders with a Moscavian grandparent was transformed into an Owl-folk creature in a single blinding event.
The Zakonnik legal code was revised to address roosting rights, territorial disputes, and nighttime commerce for the transformed population.
The White Talon and Frosted Wing regiments were established as the backbone of the Tsardom's standing army.

items.name: Moskov
items.text: The capital city stands at the confluence of the Volga and Moskva rivers, a fortress of stone and timber.

items.name: The Cathedral of the Eternal Light
items.text: The seat of the Patriarch in Moskov's heart, crowned by gilded onion domes visible across the city.

items.name: The Shrine of First Dawn
items.text: Built at the site where the original Tsar received the Light's blessing in 412.

items.name: The Dawn Vigil
items.text: The primary daily service held at first light in cathedral chapels, centering on hymns to the Eternal Light.

items.name: Baptism by Candlelight
items.text: The rite marking a young Owl's entrance into the Church, reflecting the species' preference for dim interiors.
Nighttime commerce is the economic norm, conducted under lantern light along Moskov's streets and market squares.

items.name: The Illumination
items.text: The transformation of 994 is interpreted as the Eternal Light's ultimate revelation, raising Moscavia's children to a higher state.

items.name: The Zakonnik
items.text: The revised legal code governing roosting rights, territorial disputes over nesting spaces, and nighttime commerce.
The Church teaches that all truth is found through the Light and that darkness is the absence of divine knowledge.
Scholars study the Illumination's theological implications, though secular learning remains limited to practical disciplines.

items.name: The Tsar
items.text: The supreme ruler of the Tsardom, sitting upon a throne scaled for Owl-folk wingspans of eight feet or more.

items.name: The Patriarch of Moscavia
items.text: The supreme head of the Church, appointed by the Tsar from among senior clergy Owl-folk.

items.name: The Synod of Lanterns
items.text: The governing council of twelve senior bishops who deliberate on doctrine and canon law.

elsewhere.text: The blinding transformation of 994 reshaped every human within Moscavia's borders with a Moscavian grandparent into an Owl-folk creature, preserving their full human minds.
Pure-line Moscavians—those with unbroken bloodlines through all four grandparents—emerged as snowy owls with entirely white plumage.
Eared owls predominate in Valdmark, Keshra, and the Southern Reach, descended from diluted Moscavian bloodlines through generations of intermarriage.

elsewhere.entry: The Divine Right of the Tsar
elsewhere.target: The Divine Right of the Tsar
elsewhere.text: The Tsar rules Moscavia as the earthly steward chosen by the grace and blessing of the Church of the Eternal Light.

elsewhere.entry: The Divine Right of the Tsar
elsewhere.target: The Divine Right of the Tsar
elsewhere.text: Trade continues with Valdmark, Keshra, and the Southern Reach, though relations are complicated by the eared owl-folk populations in those lands.
The White Talon is an elite regiment of the Moscavian standing army, recruited primarily from pure-line snowy Owl-folk.
Moskov's architecture has adapted to its Owl-folk population with wider doorways, taller ceilings, and roosting platforms while retaining many pre-transformation structures.
Snowy Moscavian Owls stand close to four feet tall with entirely white plumage and smooth, unblemished pale faces.
The Church of the Eternal Light is the state religion of the Tsardom of Moscavia, centered on the belief that the Light is the source of all creation.
The Church interprets the Illumination of 994 as the ultimate revelation of the Eternal Light.

items.text: Moskov: The capital city stands at the confluence of the Volga and Moskva rivers, a fortress of stone and timber.

items.name: The Cathedral of the Eternal Light
items.text: The seat of the Patriarch in Moskov's heart, crowned by gilded onion domes visible across the city.
The Shrine of First Dawn: Built at the site where the original Tsar received the Light's blessing in 412.
The Dawn Vigil: The primary daily service held at first light in cathedral chapels, centering on hymns to the Eternal Light.

items.name: Baptism by Candlelight
items.text: The rite marking a young Owl's entrance into the Church, reflecting the species' preference for dim interiors.
Nighttime commerce is the economic norm, conducted under lantern light along Moskov's streets and market squares.
The Illumination: The transformation of 994 is interpreted as the Eternal Light's ultimate revelation, raising Moscavia's children to a higher state.

items.name: The Zakonnik
items.text: The revised legal code governing roosting rights, territorial disputes over nesting spaces, and nighttime commerce.
The Church teaches that all truth is found through the Light and that darkness is the absence of divine knowledge.
Scholars study the Illumination's theological implications, though secular learning remains limited to practical disciplines.

items.name: The Tsar
items.text: The supreme ruler of the Tsardom, sitting upon a throne scaled for Owl-folk wingspans of eight feet or more.
The Patriarch of Moscavia: The supreme head of the Church, appointed by the Tsar from among senior clergy Owl-folk.
The Synod of Lanterns: The governing council of twelve senior bishops who deliberate on doctrine and canon law.

new_items.name: The Diaconate
new_items.text: Deacons assist parish priests in liturgical duties and tend to the material needs of church properties.

new_items.name: Provincial Archbishops
new_items.text: Archbishops oversee clusters of parishes within each of Moscavia's five administrative regions, bridging local and national Church governance.

new_items.name: The Order of the Radiant Eye
new_items.text: An elite clerical order dedicated to scholarly study and the preservation of canonical texts, stationed at the Cathedral of the Eternal Light.
Clergy candidates undergo a minimum of seven years of training, beginning with novitiate service and culminating in examination before the Synod of Lanterns.

elsewhere.text: The Patriarch serves as the spiritual head of the Church and the senior member of the Synod of Lanterns by right of office.
The Synod convenes at least twice annually in Moskov, with extraordinary sessions called by the Patriarch or Tsar as needed.
Pilgrimages to the Shrine of First Dawn are considered especially meritorious during the weeks leading up to the Festival of the Solstice Flame.

new_items.name: The Diaconate of the White Feather
new_items.text: Awarded to clergy who demonstrate exceptional devotion, this honor permits wear of a white feather at collar, marking them as personal emissaries of the Patriarch.

new_items.name: Provincial Vicars
new_items.text: Appointed by the Synod to oversee clusters of parishes across Moscavia's rural territories, they report directly to the Synod on matters of doctrine and moral discipline.

new_items.name: The Order of the Radiant Quill
new_items.text: Scholars and scribes tasked with maintaining the Church's canonical texts and recording oral traditions as supplementary revelation, based in the scriptorium beneath the Cathedral.
Deacons assist parish priests in conducting services, tending candlelit chapels, and preparing young Owls for Baptism by Candlelight.
Archdeacons serve as the immediate supervisors of parish priests within each of Moskov's ecclesiastical districts, evaluating their performance and resolving local disputes.

elsewhere.text: The Patriarch's marble seat in the Cathedral of the Eternal Light was consecrated during the Great Synod of Moskov in 687.
The Synod meets four times annually—at the equinoxes and solstices—to review provincial reports and amend canon law as needed by the changing needs of Owl-folk society.

result.text: Deacons serve as the intermediate rank between parish priests and bishops, assisting in liturgical duties and administering to the sick.

result.name: The Order of the Silver Candle
result.text: An elite monastic order tasked with preserving and transcribing sacred texts, the Order of the Silver Candle maintains scriptoria across Moscavia.

result.name: Provincial Exarchs
result.text: Each of the Tsardom's twelve provinces is overseen by an Exarch appointed by the Patriarch, who enforces canon law and coordinates parish networks.

result.name: The Office of the Sacristan
result.text: Every church maintains a Sacristan who tends to the candlelight, holy vessels, and vestments essential to Owl-folk worship.

result.text: Only the Patriarch or his authorized Exarchs may consecrate a new church building, marking it as a vessel of the Light through prayer and anointing.

new_items.text: Each of Moscavia's twelve dioceses is governed by an Archpriest, who oversees all parish churches within its borders.

new_items.name: The Order of the Radiant Wing
new_items.text: A monastic order of warrior-priests who guard holy sites and serve as the Church's military arm during times of crisis.

new_items.name: Provincial Deacons
new_items.text: Assistants to parish priests who prepare sacraments, tend to the sick, and carry messages between parishes and the diocese.
Bishops must be at least forty years old and have served as parish priests for no fewer than fifteen years before being considered for the Synod.

elsewhere.text: The texts include a dedicated section on the proper conduct of the Dawn Vigil, specifying which hymns must be sung and the order of candle-lighting.
The Cathedral houses the Patriarch's marble seat and serves as the meeting hall for the Synod of Lanterns during their twice-yearly sessions.

new_items.name: Kethara's Workshop
new_items.text: A crumbling stone tower in the Greywood Valley, said to be where Aelberth compiled his Codex.

new_items.text: The ruined foundation of the Greyholm Archive, now a memorial and restricted site.

new_items.name: The Weavers' Crossing

elsewhere.text: The Codex was compiled not in Stonehold's great halls but in the modest workshop of a craftsman on the valley's edge.
The Shattered Library of Greyholm remains under Conclave jurisdiction, its ruins periodically searched for surviving fragments.
The Bone Garden of Vethara is considered a satellite site of the Ashenmere tradition, though it predates the caves themselves.
Kethara's Workshop contains deepcarved runes on its interior walls, among the oldest surviving examples outside Ashenmere.

new_items.text: A root system beneath Ashenmere that glows faintly and hums at a low frequency, believed to have been shaped by ancient cave-inscribers into a living rune lattice.

new_items.name: Keth's Workshop
new_items.text: A small stone building in Stonehold's outer ward where Master Weaver Keth of Ashenmere conducts private research into the third resonance law.

new_items.name: The Shattered Index
new_items.text: A fragmentary manuscript surviving from the Greyholm Archive, containing cross-referenced entries on rune combinations that no longer correspond to any known text.
The Conclave maintains a quarantine ward in Stonehold for materials that have absorbed corrupted runes, preventing their contamination of other inscriptions.

elsewhere.text: The Pale Root extends for at least two miles beneath the northern chambers of Ashenmere, and weavers believe it may connect to chambers that have never been mapped.
Keth's Workshop sits adjacent to the outer wall of Stonehold's inner citadel, accessible only through a rune-locked gate.

new_items.name: Boyar Duma
new_items.text: The Boyar Duma is the Tsardom's supreme council of noble Owl-folk advisors, convened by the Tsar to deliberate on matters of state, taxation, and territorial disputes.

new_items.name: Provincial Voevoda
new_items.text: Each of the Tsardom's twelve provinces is governed by a voevoda, a military governor appointed by the Tsar who oversees local administration, justice, and defense.

new_items.name: The Night Watch
new_items.text: The Night Watch is Moskov's civilian militia, staffing checkpoint towers and patrolling the city's streets after dusk to maintain order during peak commerce hours.
All military officers above the rank of sotnik must be confirmed by the Church of the Eternal Light to ensure loyalty to both the Tsar and the faith.

elsewhere.text: The Frosted Wing maintains permanent garrison posts along the Oka River line, the traditional boundary marker between Moscavia and Keshra.
White Talon recruits undergo a grueling three-year training period at the Barabansk Fortress academy before seeing active border duty.
The Tsar is both the supreme military commander and the head of the Boyar Duma, with the power to overrule any council vote by decree.

new_items.name: The Grand Marshal's Court
new_items.text: The highest military council in Moscavia, presiding over all regiments and border garrisons from the Tsar's palace in Moskov.

new_items.name: Provincial Roost-Wardens
new_items.text: Locally appointed Owl-folk officials responsible for adjudicating roosting disputes, enforcing the Zakonnik, and maintaining nighttime order in each province.

new_items.name: The Border Talons
new_items.text: A network of rapid-response squadrons stationed at key points along the Valdmark and Keshra frontiers, serving as the military's eyes and striking arm for frontier incidents.

The Tsar appoints provincial governors—called *namestniki*—to administer each of Moscavia's twelve provinces, collecting tribute, maintaining roads, and commanding local militias under the Grand Marshal's authority.

result.text: The highest military council in Moscavia, presiding over all regiments and border garrisons from the Tsar's palace in Moskov.

result.name: Provincial Roost-Wardens
result.text: Locally appointed Owl-folk officials responsible for adjudicating roosting disputes, enforcing the Zakonnik, and maintaining nighttime order in each province.

result.name: The Border Talons
result.text: A network of rapid-response squadrons stationed at key points along the Valdmark and Keshra frontiers, serving as the military's eyes and striking arm for frontier incidents.

The Tsar appoints provincial governors—called *namestniki*—to administer each of Moscavia's twelve provinces, collecting tribute, maintaining roads, and commanding local militias under the Grand Marshal's authority.

new_items.name: Boyar Council
new_items.text: The Boyar Council advises the Tsar on matters of state, composed of senior nobles and military commanders who deliberate in the Kremlin's amber-halled chamber.

new_items.name: Roosting Commissariat
new_items.text: The Roosting Commissariat enforces Zakonnik provisions on nesting disputes and dwelling allocations across Moskov's concentric districts.

new_items.name: Border Marshals
new_items.text: Border Marshals command garrison posts along the Valdmark and Keshra frontiers, coordinating with regiments like the Frosted Wing and White Talon.
Each province of Moscavia is governed by a Namestnik, a governor appointed by the Tsar to oversee local administration, tax collection, and regiment recruitment.

elsewhere.text: The Frosted Wing operates under the command of a Border Marshal stationed at the southeastern fortress of Ryazan, conducting nighttime patrols of the steppe frontier.
The White Talon maintains its headquarters within the Kremlin itself, reporting directly to the Tsar's court rather than to any regional commander.

The Zakonnik's revised chapters on roosting rights include provisions for communal nesting houses in Moskov's inner districts, where families without private elevated spaces may claim designated roosting platforms.

creates.name: Architecture of Moskov

facts.text: The buildings of Moskov are constructed primarily from fieldstone and oak timber, materials chosen for their durability against the harsh northern winters and their availability from the surrounding forests of the upper Volga basin.

Onion domes, gilded or painted in deep reds and golds, crown the city's churches and monastic buildings, their distinctive rounded forms visible across the skyline and serving as landmarks for Owl-folk navigating home through fog or darkness.

Roofs throughout the city are steeply pitched with overhanging eaves, designed to shed heavy snowfalls that would otherwise collapse flatter structures, and they are traditionally painted in dark reds and greens with gold trim.

Windows in Moskovian buildings are large and numerous, set high in walls to allow moonlight and candlelight to penetrate deep into interior spaces, accommodating the nocturnal habits of the Owl-folk who inhabit them.
Many structures feature wide, elevated porches and open galleries along their facades, providing sheltered perches where Owl-folk can rest, socialize, or survey the streets below in safety.

The Kremlin's walls are built from massive blocks of local limestone quarried from the banks of the Volga, with towers rising at each corner and along the curtain walls at regular intervals, each tower topped with a pointed roof and weather vane.

Interior spaces are designed with high, vaulted ceilings to accommodate the tallest of the Owl-folk, and rooms are organized around large central hearths or stove-hearths that serve as both heat sources and communal gathering points during winter nights.

Wooden lattice screens and decorated shutters, carved with geometric patterns and religious motifs, are fitted to windows and balconies throughout the city, allowing ventilation while maintaining privacy.

The Tsar's palace within the Kremlin combines stone foundations with elaborate timber construction above, its halls hung with icon screens and illuminated by chandeliers of wrought iron holding dozens of beeswax candles.

Market stalls and trade halls in the merchant quarters are built with open-air ground floors shaded by canvas awnings and enclosed upper galleries, allowing nighttime commerce to proceed even during summer rainstorms.

Bridges across the Moskva and Volga within the city are reinforced with stone piers and timber decks, wide enough for carts and laden birds to cross side by side, and lit by rows of iron lantern brackets carrying oil lamps from dusk until dawn.

elsewhere.text: The radial street plan of Moskov means that the city's concentric neighborhoods each have a character shaped by proximity to the Kremlin, with stone fortifications giving way to timber merchant halls and residential quarters in the outer rings.

The Cathedral's interior is designed with a cavernous, candlelit nave where the light of thousands of flames reflects off gilded icon screens and the polished surfaces of its onion domes, creating an atmosphere intended to evoke the Eternal Light itself.

The rite's architecture demands shallow stone font basins built into church floors, wide enough for a young Owl to stand in while surrounded by water, with tall candelabras positioned at each corner to cast flickering light across the ceremony.

The Zakonnik includes specific building codes governing the minimum dimensions of roosting spaces in all residential structures, ensuring compliance with the physical needs of Owl-folk tenancy as defined by law.

creates.name: The Architecture of Moskov

facts.text: The buildings of Moskov are designed to accommodate the nocturnal habits of the Owl-folk, with deep eaves and high windows that admit the moonlight while shielding interiors from harsh daytime glare.

Stone foundations and walls of rough-cut limestone and granite form the structural core of every important building in the city, a tradition inherited from the pre-Owl-folk settlements that once stood on the same ground.

Timber framing of spruce and birch is used for upper stories, roof structures, and interior partitions, giving buildings a lighter skeletal frame over the heavy stone base — a technique perfected by Moscavian master builders in the decades following the Blinding Transformation.

Onion domes, gilded or painted in deep reds and golds, crown the city's churches and monasteries, their rounded forms inspired by the traditional nesting hollows of the Great Horned Owl revered in early Moscavian spiritual practice.

Roofs are steeply pitched and shingled with wooden planks or split birch bark, designed to shed the heavy snows of northern winters while creating generous loft spaces used as roosting chambers for Owl-folk families.

Windows in Moskov buildings are tall and narrow, with shutters that can be sealed tight during the day and thrown wide open at night, fitted with thin membranes of oiled parchment to muffle wind while allowing air to circulate through living quarters.

The Kremlin's outer walls are faced with massive blocks of white limestone quarried from the Ural foothills, a material so prized that its use in lesser buildings is restricted under the Zakonnik's building codes.

Perch-balconies — narrow wooden platforms projecting from exterior walls at regular intervals — are a defining feature of residential buildings throughout Moskov, providing resting spots for Owl-folk traveling along streets at night.

Interior spaces are organized around a central hearth-hall with a stone fireplace large enough to roast game birds, surrounded by smaller sleeping alcoves curtained off with heavy wool tapestries for privacy and warmth.

Church interiors are deliberately kept dim, with thick walls and few windows, so that the thousands of candles burning inside create an atmosphere of warm, enveloping glow that Owl-folk find as natural as daylight.

Market stalls and trading halls along the Volga riverbank use open-sided stone pavilions covered by canvas awnings that can be retracted in fair weather, allowing Owl-folk merchants to conduct business under the stars.

The Tsar's palace in the Kremlin combines fortress-like stone battlements on its lower levels with ornate timber galleries and gilded onion domes above, symbolizing the union of military strength and spiritual authority that defines the Tsardom's ideology.

elsewhere.text: The radial street plan of Moskov, centered on the Kremlin, means that the tallest buildings and grandest domes are always visible from the riverbanks, projecting the city's power and piety to arriving merchants and diplomats.

The Cathedral's interior dimensions — its vaulted stone ceilings and wide nave — are proportioned to allow hundreds of Owl-folk to perch comfortably on its wooden rafters during major services, making the congregation literally suspended above the altar.
The candlelit baptismal fonts in parish churches across Moskov are set into shallow stone basins carved to accommodate the wide, taloned feet of young Owl-folk standing in the blessed water.

creates.name: Zakonnik

facts.text: The Zakonnik is the comprehensive legal code of the Tsardom of Moscavia, revised in the years following the Illumination of 994 to govern the practical needs of a society of Owl-folk.

The code establishes clear regulations for roosting rights, ensuring that every Owl-folk citizen has legal claim to a designated nesting space, whether within private residences, communal roost-houses, or public buildings adapted for nighttime habitation.

Nesting disputes—over territory, proximity, noise, and structural modifications to roosting spaces—are adjudicated through a hierarchy of local magistrates and regional courts, with final appeals heard by the Tsar's judicial council in Moskov.

The Zakonnik mandates that all new construction within the Tsardom must include roosting platforms and perching ledges sized for the occupying Owl-folk population, with minimum dimensions prescribed by the Bureau of Public Works.

Nighttime trade is the economic backbone of the Tsardom, and the Zakonnik regulates it extensively: market hours are defined as dusk to dawn in all towns and cities, and street lighting along major thoroughfares is mandated to accommodate commerce and pedestrian traffic.

Merchants operating after midnight must display illuminated signage visible at a distance of no less than thirty paces, and all contracts of sale executed between the hours of midnight and the third bell before dawn carry the same legal weight as those conducted earlier in the night.

The code addresses the rights of Owl-folk to fly freely within city limits, while imposing restrictions on aerial passage over crowded market squares, church services, and the Tsar's palace grounds during ceremonial occasions.

Penalties for violations of the Zakonnik range from fines levied in silver kopecks to temporary confiscation of roosting rights for repeat offenders, with the most serious disputes—those involving bodily harm or destruction of nesting structures—subject to criminal prosecution before the Tsar's court.

The code was drafted by a council of legal scholars convened by the Tsar in the years immediately following the Illumination, drawing on pre-994 Moscavian legal tradition while adapting it to the new biological realities of the population.
Copies of the Zakonnik are maintained in every parish church throughout the Tsardom, written in silver ink on dark vellum as prescribed by the Church of the Eternal Light for all official documents.

The Zakonnik is considered living law: amendments are proposed by regional assemblies and ratified by the Tsar in consultation with the Patriarch of the Church, ensuring that the code evolves alongside the needs of the Owl-folk society.

elsewhere.text: The Zakonnik serves as the Tsardom's primary legal framework, revised after the Illumination of 994 to address the unique needs of an Owl-folk society, including roosting rights, nesting disputes, and nighttime commerce regulations.
The Zakonnik is enforced throughout Moskov, the capital city, where the Tsar's judicial council hears final appeals in matters of roosting rights and commercial disputes.

facts.text: The Zakonnik is the comprehensive legal code of the Tsardom of Moscavia, revised in the years following the Illumination of 994 to address the practical and legal needs of a society of Owl-folk.
The revised Zakonnik governs matters of roosting rights, territorial disputes over nesting spaces, and the regulation of nighttime commerce—the economic norm in a kingdom of nocturnal beings.
The code establishes clear legal frameworks for property disputes involving elevated nesting platforms, which Owl-folk instinctively seek out and fiercely defend as territory.
Nighttime trade is regulated under the Zakonnik to ensure fair commerce, with markets mandated to remain open from dusk to dawn across all towns and cities within the Tsardom.

The Zakonnik includes provisions for the construction and legal recognition of roosting platforms in public buildings, workplaces, and residential structures, with minimum size requirements based on the occupant's wingspan.
Disputes over nesting rights are adjudicated by local magistrates appointed under the Zakonnik, with appeals available to regional courts presided over by Owl-folk judges.

The code addresses the unique legal challenges of Owl-folk society, including noise regulations during daylight hours when the majority of the population sleeps, and liability for disturbances to roosting neighbors.

The Zakonnik was drafted by a council of legal scholars convened by the Tsar in the years immediately following the Illumination, drawing upon pre-994 Moscavian law while adapting it for the transformed population.

Public buildings constructed before the Illumination have been retrofitted under Zakonnik mandates to include wider doorways, taller ceilings, and structural reinforcements to support roosting platforms weighing several hundred pounds.
The Zakonnik also regulates the trade of materials essential to Owl-folk life, including furs, timber for nesting, and candles—staples of the nocturnal economy.

Copies of the revised Zakonnik are maintained in every parish church in Moscavia, where they are read aloud in the dim, candlelit interiors that suit Owl-folk eyes, ensuring the code is accessible to all citizens.

elsewhere.text: The Zakonnik serves as the legal backbone of the Tsardom of Moscavia, ensuring that the vast northern kingdom's governance adapts seamlessly to the transformed Owl-folk population.

creates.name: The Runeweavers' Oath

facts.text: Every Runeweaver must swear the Oath upon entering the craft, typically at the age of formal apprenticeship completion, before the Conclave's senior weavers in Stonehold.
The Oath binds the weaver to serve the craft and the material equally, never placing personal gain or ambition above the integrity of the rune.
Breaking any article of the Oath results in immediate expulsion from the Conclave and the revocation of all rune-licenses, effectively ending the weaver's career.
A weaver who breaks the Oath and refuses to confess may be hunted by the Conclave's Wardens of the Vow, who have authority to strip inscribed work of its power as penance.
The Oath was first codified during the founding of the Conclave in 642, though oral traditions suggest Runeweavers swore informal vows as far back as the earliest cave inscriptions at Ashenmere.
One of the Oath's central articles mirrors the Doctrine of Cost: the weaver must acknowledge that every inscription is an exchange, and they may not deceive a client about what the rune will demand.
The Oath explicitly forbids the inscription of runes for profit alone, reinforcing the principle that Runework serves purpose, not commerce.
Weavers who take the Oath are required to renew their vows publicly every five years at the Conclave's autumn gathering in Stonehold.
The Oath's exact wording is kept in a sealed vault within Stonehold and is not publicly known; only licensed weavers may hear it recited in full during their swearing ceremony.

The Prohibition of the Flesh Rune is considered the most serious breach of the Oath, carrying not just exile but a formal curse that renders the offending weaver unable to channel rune-energy for the rest of their life.
Some historians believe the Greyholm Archive held a complete record of every oath sworn since 642, and that its destruction in 888 means many early oaths are now irrecoverably lost.
The Oath includes a clause acknowledging that the material itself has a right to refuse the inscription, echoing the belief that forcing a rune onto an unwilling substrate is a sin against the craft.

elsewhere.text: The Runeweavers' Oath is the ethical foundation upon which all licensed Runework is performed, and its articles directly inform several of the craft's governing principles.
Stonehold serves as both the seat of the Conclave and the traditional site where the Oath is sworn and renewed.
The Greyholm Archive once contained a master register of every oath sworn since the Conclave's founding, a loss that scholars still mourn.

facts.text: Every aspiring Runeweaver must swear the Oath upon completion of their apprenticeship and before they are admitted to the craft as a full practitioner.
The Oath is spoken aloud before the assembled Conclave at Stonehold, with the weaver's hands resting on an unmarked stone called the Witness.
The Oath binds the weaver to serve the craft with integrity, to never inscribe a rune for profit alone, and to respect the material upon which they work.
A Runeweaver who breaks the Oath is subject to trial by the Conclave and, if found guilty, may be stripped of their rank and exiled from all sanctioned practice.
The original text of the Oath was written by the Conclave's first Speaker, Aldric of Greyholm, and was among the works destroyed in the Burning of 888.
The current recitation of the Oath is maintained through oral tradition and three surviving partial transcripts, each housed in different Conclave libraries.
The Oath includes a clause acknowledging that the weaver's own life force may be called upon to fuel an inscription, and that this sacrifice must be made freely, never coerced.
Apprentices who refuse to swear the Oath are dismissed from training and forbidden from practicing Runework in any Conclave-recognized territory.
The Oath does not expire; once sworn, it holds for the weaver's entire life. There is no known ritual to release a weaver from its binding.
Weavers who travel to the southern kingdoms sometimes find that local customs allow minor deviations from the Oath's strictures, a point of ongoing debate within the Conclave.
The Witness stone upon which the Oath is sworn is said to be a fragment of limestone taken from the walls of Ashenmere, though this claim has never been verified.

The Oath's connection to Ashenmere is maintained through the tradition of the Witness stone, linking the oldest known runes to the oldest known vow.
The destruction of the Greyholm Archive in 888 forced the Conclave to rely on memory and scattered fragments to preserve the exact wording of the Oath.

facts.text: The Ashenmere Caves are a vast network of limestone caves and subterranean galleries carved into the northern foothills of the Greymarch Mountains, stretching across roughly twelve square miles of twisting passages, open chambers, and deep vertical shafts.

The cave walls are coated in a fine layer of volcanic ash — the source of the 'ashen' in the caves' name — deposited over millennia by eruptions from the Greymarch caldera to the south, which has long since gone dormant.

The air inside is cool and still, carrying a faint mineral scent mixed with the musty smell of ancient stone. Water drips through stalactites in some chambers, while others are bone-dry, their floors cracked and pale as old bone.

The first systematic excavation began in 947, when a Runeweaver named Maren Ashwick discovered a chamber near the eastern entrance covered floor to ceiling in intact runic inscriptions dating back at least two thousand years.
Since 947, approximately one-third of the cave system has been mapped and accessible to scholars, though only a fraction of the inscriptions have been fully transcribed and analyzed.
Before 947, local shepherds and miners had known about the caves for generations but regarded them as dangerous and unremarkable, never venturing past the first few chambers.

The caves contain evidence of at least four distinct periods of rune inscription, spanning from crude, deeply carved glyphs in the oldest chambers to finely detailed etchings in the more recently used passages.

Some chambers appear to have been deliberately sealed off by the ancient weavers themselves, using inscribed stone barriers that resist any attempt to break them apart — a technique not yet fully understood by modern weavers.
The oldest inscriptions in the deepest chambers predate the First Codex of Aelberth by over a millennium and employ glyphs and syntactic structures found nowhere else in the known rune tradition.

The site is managed by a permanent research settlement of roughly forty weavers and scholars, known informally as the Ashenmere Circle, who live in prefabricated stone shelters built near the main entrance.

Access to the inner chambers is restricted to weavers of at least journeyman rank, and all visitors must swear an oath of non-interference with the inscriptions — touching the walls without authorization is strictly forbidden.
The caves have yielded several fragments of what scholars believe may be a pre-Aelberthic rune grammar, potentially rewriting the understanding of how the art was practiced in its earliest centuries.

elsewhere.text: The Ashenmere Caves are recognized as the single most important archaeological site in the entire rune tradition, and their ongoing excavation is considered the most significant effort to recover knowledge lost during the Burning of Greyholm in 888.

Many of the Ashenmere inscriptions appear to have been created using a form of deepcarving — runes etched well below the surface of the limestone — which accounts for their extraordinary durability over thousands of years.
The destruction of the Greyholm Archive in 888 made the Ashenmere discoveries all the more critical, as the caves now hold what may be the largest surviving body of pre-888 rune knowledge.

The inscriptions found in Ashenmere suggest that the ancient weavers understood the Doctrine of Cost in a more nuanced way than modern weavers do, with some glyphs appearing to draw energy from the stone itself rather than from the weaver or the material alone.

facts.text: The Ashenmere Caves are a vast network of limestone caves and subterranean galleries nestled in the northern foothills of the Greymarch Mountains.
The cave walls are coated in a fine layer of mineral ash—calcium sulfate deposits that give the system its name and its distinctive grey-white hue.
The earliest known runic inscriptions were carved into these walls over a span of centuries, beginning at least as early as 2000 before the current calendar.
In 947, a party of Runeweavers led by the scholar Maren Duvaine re-entered the caves and confirmed that the inscriptions were genuine and far older than anything in the surviving Greyholm records.

The cave system extends for over forty miles beneath the mountains, with some passages so narrow that only a single person can pass through, and others opening into chambers large enough to hold a cathedral.
The air inside is cool and still, with a faint sulphurous smell near the deeper passages where geothermal vents heat the stone.
Water drips continuously from the ceiling in most sections, and pools collect in the lower chambers, often around clusters of the oldest inscriptions.
Only about a quarter of the known passages have been fully mapped and excavated; the remaining three-quarters remain inaccessible due to unstable rock formations and flooding.
Access to the Ashenmere Caves is restricted by the Runeweavers' Conclave; unlicensed visitors are barred by order of the Conclave to prevent unauthorized disturbance of the inscriptions.

The inscriptions found here employ a rune dialect that pre-dates Aelberth's standardization by over a millennium, and their resonance properties have challenged long-held assumptions about how runes interact with stone.

elsewhere.text: The Ashenmere inscriptions are considered the foundational evidence that the art of runeweaving predates all written records by centuries.
The Ashenmere inscriptions demonstrate deepcarving techniques of extraordinary refinement, with glyphs etched up to three inches below the surface of the limestone.
The destruction of the Greyholm Archive in 888 makes the Ashenmere Caves one of the few surviving sources of pre-Conclave rune knowledge.
The Runeweavers' Conclave maintains a permanent research station in the outer chambers of the Ashenmere Caves, staffed by weavers on rotating assignment.

facts.text: On the longest night of winter, every parish in Moscavia lights a great bonfire in its square as a communal act of devotion to the Eternal Light.
The festival marks the turning point of the year, when the nights begin to shorten and the Light's influence over the world grows stronger once more.
Parish priests are responsible for preparing the bonfire site in the square, consecrating the woodpile, and leading the community in prayer before the flames are lit.
Families gather around the fire and share a communal meal, while children are often given small candles of their own to carry in procession around the blaze.
The flames are meant to mirror the Eternal Light's warmth, pushing back the literal and spiritual darkness of the longest night.
In Moskov, the bonfire in the great square before the Cathedral of the Eternal Light is lit first, and its flames are carried outward from parish to parish across the city.
The festival includes hymns and readings from scripture, with the Patriarch or a senior bishop presiding at the capital's central fire.
Owl-folk consider the festival a reminder that the Light transformed their ancestors, and that warmth and community are the highest expressions of divine love.
The bonfire wood is gathered in the weeks leading up to the festival, with each household contributing logs that have been blessed by the local parish priest.
The festival strengthens communal bonds within each parish, reinforcing the Church's role as the center of Owl-folk life.
In remote villages far from Moskov, the Solstice Flame is sometimes the only major celebration of the year, making it the most anticipated event in the parish calendar.

elsewhere.text: The Festival of the Solstice Flame is one of the Church's most cherished ceremonies, reinforcing the doctrine that the Eternal Light conquers all darkness.
Parish priests view the festival as both a spiritual duty and a moment of deep personal fulfillment, as they guide their communities through the night's prayers and rituals.

facts.text: On the longest night of winter, every parish in Moscavia lights a great bonfire in its central square as part of the Church of the Eternal Light's annual celebration of the Solstice Flame.
The festival marks the turning point of the year, when the nights begin to shorten and the Eternal Light's influence is believed to grow stronger over the darkness.
Each bonfire is lit at dusk from a single flame carried by a parish priest, who kindles it using a taper traced back to the great hearth in the Cathedral of the Eternal Light in Moskov.
Owl-folk gather in their parish squares throughout the night, singing hymns, sharing food, and bearing witness to the Light's enduring presence even at the darkest time of year.

The bonfire is built from twelve logs, each one representing one of the months of the year, with the center log left unlit until midnight — the symbolic heart of winter — when the patriarch in Moskov signals its kindling.
Children of the parish are given small candles at the festival's end, which they carry home to light their family hearths, extending the Light's blessing into every household.
Parish priests are responsible for organizing the festival locally, preparing the bonfire site, arranging the hymn-singing, and ensuring the flame is carried properly from the cathedral chain.

In Moskov itself, the bonfire in the great square before the Cathedral of the Eternal Light is lit by the Patriarch in a ceremony attended by the Tsar and Tsarina, the Synod of Lanterns, and thousands of Owl-folk from across the realm.

The festival serves as a reminder that the Eternal Light never truly wanes, even in the longest darkness, and that the Owl-folk's transformation was the Light's promise that no shadow can overcome its radiance.
Villages and towns that lack a formal parish church still observe the festival, gathering around bonfires in their market squares with the blessing of the nearest parish priest.
The Festival of the Solstice Flame reinforces the Church's doctrine that the Eternal Light is the source of all enduring hope, and that darkness — both literal and spiritual — is temporary.

elsewhere.text: The Festival of the Solstice Flame is one of the Church's oldest and most widely observed ceremonies, dating back to the founding of the faith in 412 and maintained without interruption ever since.
The festival elevates the parish priest's role in the community, making him the visible link between the central authority of the Church in Moskov and the local Owl-folk families he serves.

facts.text: The White Talon is the most elite military regiment of the Tsardom of Moscavia, recruited exclusively from pure-line snowy Owl-folk of unbroken bloodline.

Every soldier in the White Talon traces their lineage through four pure Moscavian grandparents, ensuring their snowy plumage and the physical characteristics that make the regiment's tactics possible.
The regiment's name, 'White Talon,' refers both to the snowy plumage of its soldiers and to the precision and lethality of its strikes against border threats.
Members of the White Talon stand close to four feet tall with pure white plumage and smooth, unblemished pale faces, making them visually distinctive even among Moscavia's Owl-folk population.

The regiment is renowned for conducting swift, decisive border actions—rapidly deploying to threatened frontier positions, striking enemy forces with overwhelming speed, and withdrawing before a conventional force can respond.
White Talon soldiers are trained from youth in both aerial combat and ground tactics, with an emphasis on nocturnal operations that exploit the Owl-folk's natural sensitivity to darkness and sound.
The regiment patrols the western border of Moscavia, facing the kingdom of Valdmark, where eared owl-folk populations and residual human communities create ongoing security concerns.

Each soldier of the White Talon possesses a wingspan of approximately eight to nine feet, enabling powerful sustained flight for reconnaissance, pursuit, and rapid redeployment across the northern forests and steppe.
The regiment's command structure mirrors that of the broader Moscavian military, with officers selected through a rigorous competitive process that tests both combat skill and strategic acumen.

White Talon operatives are known for their near-silent approach in flight, able to descend upon enemy positions with barely a whisper of wind through their feathers, striking before alarms can be raised.

The regiment's barracks and training grounds are located in fortified positions along the western frontier, designed with elevated roosting spaces and reinforced stone architecture adapted for Owl-folk habitation.
Service in the White Talon is considered the highest military honor available to pure-line Moscavian Owl-folk, and acceptance into the regiment is a matter of profound family pride.

elsewhere.text: The White Talon serves as a frontline defense force for the Tsardom's western border, protecting against incursions from Valdmark and ensuring the security of the northern frontier forests.
The Frosted Wing is a sister regiment to the White Talon, patrolling the southern and southeastern borders of Moscavia against threats from Keshra and the Southern Reach.
